Discretization bins:\n  - 0:  < -50 cm\n  - 1: -50 to -10 cm\n  - 2: -10 cm to < 0 cm\n  - 3: 0 cm\n  - 4: >0 cm to +10 cm\n  - 5: +10 to +50 cm\n  - 6: > +50 cm\n- Absolute position in corridor, time-varying. list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_sample_out.txt`\n397\t  a. Check input ranges and output value distributions against expectations from reference texts.\n410\t\n411\t**Done when**: \n412\t- `/app/sample_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\n413\t- `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\n414\t- Processing plots show no anomalies\n415\t- Document sample statistics in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 7\"\n416\t\n417\t**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 8 until `/app/sample_data.pkl` and `/app/verification_sample_out.txt` files exist, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 7 is filled in. \n418\t\n419\t---\n420\t\n421\t### Step 8: Sample Decoder Training\n422\t\n423\t**Goal**: Verify the decoder runs successfully on sample data.\n424\t\n425\t**Actions**:\n426\t1. Explain why each warning could not be fixed in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \n474\t\n475\t**Check 2: Construct sanity checks**\n476\t- Develop at least one sanity check each on neural, input, and output data.\n477\t- These must involve loading in the original data files (NOT through your conversion code).\n478\t- Construct comparison tests and criteria using `np.allclose()`. \n479\t- These tests can be spot-checks of the data, e.g. neural activity at trial 5, timepoint 10, neuron 3. \n480\t- Fix all mismatches/sanity check failures. \n481\t- Document your sanity checks to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \n482\t\n483\t**Check 3: Reference code comparison**\n484\t- Compare your code to the reference code and methods. \n485\t- For each major processing step — (a) data loading, (b) neuron/trial filtering, (c) temporal alignment, (d) binning, (e) input construction, (f) output construction — identify the corresponding code in your script and in the reference, and compare the logic. \n486\t- Check whether you use the same variables, filtering, and processing as the reference code. \n487\t- Fix any mismatches. \n488\t- Document your comparisons in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \n489\t- Explain your reasoning for any differences in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`.\n490\t\n491\t**Check 4: Key statistics comparison**\n492\t- Verify that key statistics (number of animals, sessions, trials, neurons, input and output ranges, output distributions) match information available in the reference paper. \n493\t- Write code to investigate any discrepancies. \n494\t- Fix any discovered issues. \n495\t- Document your comparisons in `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \n496\t\n497\t**Check 5: Check for edge cases**\n498\t- Check for off-by-one errors at the beginning/ends of trials, sessions, and subjects, or in definitions of the inputs and outputs. \n499\t- There may be minor issues in the data that your code must handle. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\n534\t\n535\t**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\n536\t- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\n537\t- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \n538\t- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \n539\t\n540\t**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to paper**\n541\t- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference paper\n542\t- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the paper's accuracy for each variable\n543\t- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \n544\t- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n545\t\n546\t**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n547\t- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n548\t\n549\t**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n550\t1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\n551\t2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\n552\t3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\n553\t4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \n554\t5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and paper. \n555\t\n556\t**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n557\t1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n558\t2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n559\t3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n560\t4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n561\t\n562\t**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \n563\t\n564\t**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 12\".\n565\t\n566\t---\n567\t\n568\t### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n569\t\n570\t**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\n571\t\n572\t**Actions**:\n573\t- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\n574\t  - Key decisions and rationale\n575\t  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\n576\t  - Validation results and tables\n577\t  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\n578\t- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\n579\t  - Dataset description\n580\t  - How to load and use the converted data\n581\t  - Output format specification\n582\t  - Key statistics\n583\t- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\n584\t- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\n585\t\n586\t**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\n587\t\n588\t---\n589\t\n590\t## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\n591\t\n592\t**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. Neuroscience Data Specifics\n843\t- **Spike times vs. firing rates**: Decide on appropriate binning for spike data\n844\t- **Trial alignment**: Align trials to meaningful events (stimulus onset, movement, etc.)\n845\t- **Time windows**: Choose appropriate pre/post-event windows\n846\t- **Neuron curation**: Choose filtering criteria for the quality of each neuron's recording based on reference texts\n847\t- **Trial curation**: Choose quality filtering criteria for trials based on reference texts or bad or missing data\n848\t\n849\t### Computational Efficiency\n850\t- Be mindful of memory usage with large datasets\n851\t- Use appropriate data types (float32 vs. float64)\n852\t- Consider lazy loading for very large datasets\n853\t- Implement efficient array operations (vectorization)\n854\t\n855\t## Success Criteria\n856\t\n857\tA successful conversion should:\n858\t1. Discretization bins:\n  - 0:  < -50 cm\n  - 1: -50 to -10 cm\n  - 2: -10 cm to < 0 cm\n  - 3: 0 cm\n  - 4: >0 cm to +10 cm\n  - 5: +10 to +50 cm\n  - 6: > +50 cm\n- Absolute position in corridor, time-varying. Discretized into 5 equal-sized bins spanning the 450 cm track:\n  - 0: < 90 cm\n  - 1: 90 to 180 cm\n  - 2: 180 to 270 cm\n  - 3: 270 to 360 cm\n  - 4: > 360 cm\n- Speed, time-varying. Discretized into bins:\n  - 0: < 2 cm/s\n  - 1: 2-10 cm/s\n  - 2: 10-20 cm/s\n  - 3: 20-40 cm/s\n  - 4: > 40 cm/s\n- Lick, time-varying. 0 = no, 1 = yes\n- Reward zone location, per-trial. 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C\n- Reward outcome, per-trial. 0 = no, 1 = yes\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Distance to reward zone* derived from?\n297\t\n298\ti. Derived from the `position` behavior time series and the reward zone location for the current trial. To allow for some noise (of unknown source) and unrewarded tasks, I use the Viterbi algorithm to assign zones so that the rewarded positions match the known reward zones and it is uncommon to switch reward zone. \n299\t\n300\tii. The paper discusses how neural alignment is done across mice, but I ignored this to reduce complexity. \n\nii. \n```python\ndef get_sessions(subject, datadir=DATADIR):\n    subject_dir = os.path.join(datadir, f\"sub-{subject}\")\n    # parse sessions from files named sub-<subject>-<session>_behavior+ophys.nwb\n    nwb_files = [f for f in os.listdir(subject_dir) if f.endswith('.nwb')]\n    sessions = [int(f.split('_')[1].split('-')[1]) for f in nwb_files]\n    return sessions\n...\nsessions_per_subject = {subject: get_sessions(subject, datadir=args.datadir) for subject in data['subjects']}\n```\n\niii. Names of the files include a parsable `ses-<number>`, suggesting that this is a session. \n\n## 1-d. Are the data correctly split into trials? \n\ni. The start of each trial is identified based on the `behavior` variable `trial_start`. The end of each trial is identified by the `teleport` variable. I grab out data between these time points to correspond to trials. \n\nii. \n```python\ndef get_trial_starts_ends(trial_start,teleport):\n    trial_start_idx = np.nonzero(trial_start)[0]\n    is_teleport_start = (teleport[1:] > 0) & (teleport[:-1] <= 0)\n    trial_end_idx = np.nonzero(is_teleport_start)[0] + 1 \n    assert len(trial_start_idx) == len(trial_end_idx), f\"Number of trial starts ({len(trial_start_idx)}) does not match number of trial ends ({len(trial_end_idx)})\"\n    return trial_start_idx, trial_end_idx\n...\nbehavior_data = nwbfile.processing['behavior']['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series       \n...\nteleport = behavior_data['teleport'].data[:]\ntrial_start_idx, trial_end_idx = get_trial_starts_ends(behavior_data['trial_start'].data[:], teleport)\n```\n\niii. I investigated using the `trial_number` variable, but led to visually less clean data. The lengths and numbers of trials were consistent with this choice, and it matched the definition of a trial in the paper. \n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls? \n\ni. Trials with `< 50` time points were removed. \n\nii. \n```python\nfor trial in range(ntrials):\n    idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\n    if idx.sum() < min_ntimepoints:\n        print(f\"Skipping trial {trial} in subject {subject} session {session} because it has only {idx.sum() < {min_ntimepoints} time points\")\n        istrial[trial] = False\n        continue\n```\n\niii. Looking at trial lengths, there were a couple short trials that this removed, at some version of the code. \n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the final `neural` data derived from? \n\ni. Neural data is derived from the raw suite2p traces, `Fluorescence` (F) and `Neuropil` (Fneu). It is **not** the NWB's `Deconvolved` field, which is a different signal that the paper never analyzes.\n\nii. \n```python\nfluorescence_data = nwbfile.processing[\"ophys\"][\"Fluorescence\"]\nneuropil_data = nwbfile.processing[\"ophys\"][\"Neuropil\"]\nfor plane_name, plane_data in fluorescence_data.roi_response_series.items():\n    fluorescence_curr = plane_data.data[:]\n    neuropil_curr = neuropil_data.roi_response_series[plane_name].data[:]\n```\n\niii. The paper computes its own neural signal rather than using a stored one in `preprocessing.dff(F, Fneu, ..., deconvolve=True)` and stores the result as `sess.timeseries['events']`. The NWB's `Deconvolved` array is instead suite2p's own deconvolution of raw fluorescence.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed? \n\ni. dF/F is computed from F and Fneu and then deconvolved into \"events\", by a copy of the paper's own `preprocessing.dff`. Per plane: restrict to the lap samples (or lap plus teleport, depending on the session), subtract `0.7 * Fneu`, add each trial's mean neuropil back so the ratio is a true dF/F, take a maximin baseline (Gaussian smoothing with sigma 15 samples, then a 300-sample running minimum followed by a 300-sample running maximum, the Methods' 20 s window), form `(F - baseline)/|baseline|`, smooth with a 2-sample Gaussian, and deconvolve with OASIS at `tau = 0.7` and `frame_rate/n_planes`. Cells from multiple planes are pooled afterwards.\n\nWhether the baseline window may span the teleport is a per-mouse, per-day fact, copied from `teleport_metadata.py`: the laser was blanked between trials except on the days listed there, where imaging continued. It matters -- on m15 day 5, spanning the teleport widens the baseline window by 35% and moves the emitted events by ~9% (median per-cell r = 0.986).\n\nii.\n```python\ndff_curr, events_curr = dff(fluorescence_curr.T.astype(np.float64),\n                            pd.Series(trial_start_idx + 1), pd.Series(trial_end_idx + 1),\n                            f_neu=neuropil_curr.T.astype(np.float64),\n                            neuropil_method='subtract', baseline_method='maximin',\n                            subtract_baseline=True, neu_coef=0.7, tau=0.7,\n                            frame_rate=frame_rate, n_planes=nplanes, deconvolve=True,\n                            keep_teleports=keep_teleports)\n```\n\niii. This is the processing the Methods describe: \"baseline fluorescence was calculated within each trial independently using a maximin procedure with a 20 s sliding window ... dF/F was then calculated for each cell as the fluorescence minus the baseline, divided by the absolute value of the baseline, then smoothed with a two-sample (~0.129 s) s.d. Gaussian kernel. The activity rate was extracted by deconvolving dF/F with a canonical calcium kernel using the OASIS algorithm as used in Suite2p.\" The parameters are theirs: `neu_coef = 0.7` and `baseline_method = 'maximin'` from `notebooks/make_multi_anim_sess.ipynb`, `tau = 0.7` from the suite2p ops in `notebooks/suite2p_notebooks/example_m12.ipynb`.\n\nThe neural sampling rate is the same for all recordings once the multi-plane sessions are accounted for. Note that the `rate` stored on the NWB series is the scanner rate, so on the two-plane sessions it is 31 Hz and the per-plane rate -- the one that sets both the time bin and the deconvolution kernel -- is `rate/nplanes`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two filters, both the paper's. Cells are first restricted to the `iscell` ROIs, which carry suite2p's manual curation. Putative interneurons are then dropped: any cell whose dF/F correlates with the animal's running speed at r > 0.5.\n\nii. \n```python\niscell = np.array(roi_data['iscell'].to_list())[:,0] == 1\nfluorescence.append(fluorescence_curr[:,iscell])\nneuropil.append(neuropil_curr[:,iscell])\n...\nisint = is_putative_interneuron(dff_curr, speed)\nspike_data.append(events_curr[~isint].T)\n```\n\niii. `iscell` is the manual curation the Methods describe. The per-session counts approximately matches ranges in the paper. The second filter is the Methods' additional step of filtering putative interneurons. \n\n## 2-d. Timestamps are not available for the neural data, just a stored `rate`. This rate is the same for all recordings, once one accounts for the multi-plane recordings\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Distance to reward zone* derived from?\n\ni. Derived from the `position` behavior time series and the reward zone location for the current trial. The reward zone boundaries come from the `reward_zone` behavior time series. This variable is non-zero when the mouse is in the reward zone. I combine this with the position of the mouse when this is non-zero to figure out the closest reward zone. To allow for some noise (of unknown source) and unrewarded tasks, I use the Viterbi algorithm to assign zones so that the rewarded positions match the known reward zones and it is uncommon to switch reward zone. \n\nii. Assigning reward zone location for each trial: \n- Before converting, the `survey()` function was used to try to understand all the data values, including whatever is going on with the `reward_zone` variable. It first computes the position of the min and max position of the mouse when `reward_zone` is non-zero:\n```python\nbehavior_data = nwbfile.processing['behavior']['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series       \ninfo['reward_zone_positions'] = np.full((ntrials, 2), np.nan)\nposition = behavior_data['position'].data[:]\nfor trial in range(ntrials):\n    idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\n    pos_trial = position[idx]\n    reward_zone_trial = reward_zone[idx] > 0\n    if not np.any(reward_zone_trial):\n        continue\n    info['reward_zone_positions'][trial] = [np.min(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial]), np.max(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial])]\n```\nThe function `segment_reward_positions()` uses the Viterbi algorithm to assign reward zone labels so that the initial rewarded positions are close to the corresponding rewarded zone:\n```python\nreward_zone_dict = {'A': [80, 130],\n                    'B': [200, 250],\n                    'C': [320, 370]}\n...\nsigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\nzone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\ndist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\n                    startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\ndist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\nlog_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\n```\nIt also encourages the reward zone label to not change often:\n```python\npstay = .9\nlog_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\nnp.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\n```\n\niii. The paper defines reward zones A, B, C at specific position ranges. These same ranges could also be found, with some translation, in the code (required mapping X -> A, etc.). I plotted the position of the mouse when `reward_zone` was positive (note that the value was between 0 and 6 I think) to determine that the Viterbi approach would likely work, and that the start of the rewarded position was the least noisy variable to use. The class fractions were approximately 1/3 after this, so it seemed correct. \n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\n\ni. For each timepoint, compute the signed distance from the animal's position to the nearest edge of the reward zone. Distance is 0 when inside the zone, negative when before the zone, and positive when past it.  The continuous distance is then discretized into 7 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, inf]`.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_distance_to_reward_zone(position_curr, reward_zone_curr):\n    ntimepoints = len(position_curr)\n    reward_zone_range = reward_zone_dict[reward_zone_curr]\n    distance_to_reward_zone = np.zeros(ntimepoints)\n    idx_before_zone = position_curr < reward_zone_range[0]\n    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_before_zone] = position_curr[idx_before_zone] - reward_zone_range[0]\n    idx_after_zone = position_curr > reward_zone_range[1]\n    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_after_zone] = position_curr[idx_after_zone] - reward_zone_range[1]\n    return distance_to_reward_zone\n\n```\n```python\ndistance_to_reward_zone_bins = [-np.inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, np.inf]\n...\noutput_curr[0] = np.digitize(distance_to_reward_zone, distance_to_reward_zone_bins) - 1\n```\n\n\niii. This matches the paper's concept of distance relative to the reward zone. The reward zone boundaries are from `reward_zone_dict`, inspired by the reference code `Sosa_et_al_2024/src/reward_relative/behavior.py`. The `1e-6` boundary separates exactly 0 (in the zone boundary) from slightly positive. The `-1` corrects `np.digitize` to be 0-indexed.\n\n## 7-c. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. The continuous distance is discretized into 7 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, inf]`.\n\nii.\n```python\ndistance_to_reward_zone_bins = [-np.inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, np.inf]\n...\noutput_curr[0] = np.digitize(distance_to_reward_zone, distance_to_reward_zone_bins) - 1\n```\n\niii. The bin edges match the instructions. The `1e-6` boundary separates exactly 0 (in the zone boundary) from slightly positive. The `-1` corrects `np.digitize` to be 0-indexed.\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The position data and neural data share the same time indices within each trial, so no additional alignment is needed.\n\nii.\n```python\nidx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\nspike_data_curr = spike_data[idx]\nposition_curr = position[idx]\n```\n\niii. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Several cases are handled:\n- **Neural/behavior length mismatch**: If the number of neural time bins differs from behavior timestamps, data is cropped to the minimum of the two with a warning printed.\n- **Short trials**: Trials with fewer than 50 timepoints (`min_ntimepoints`) are skipped with a warning.\n- **Missing reward zone data**: Trials where `reward_zone` is never active (all zeros) get NaN positions, and the Viterbi algorithm handles these via uniform emission (assignment driven by neighboring trials' transitions).\n- **Reward timestamp alignment**: An assertion verifies reward times align within half a time bin of behavior timestamps.\n\nii.\n```python\nif T != len(timestamps):\n    print(f\"Warning: number of neural time bins ({T}) does not match number of behavior timestamps ({len(timestamps)}), cropping to the minimum of the two\")\n    T = min(T, len(timestamps))\n    spike_data = spike_data[:T]\n    timestamps = timestamps[:T]\n...\nif idx.sum() < min_ntimepoints:\n    print(f\"Skipping trial {trial}...\")\n    istrial[trial] = False\n    continue\n```\n\niii. These are defensive checks found during data exploration. The neural/behavior mismatch occurs in a small number of sessions.\n\n## 13-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. The most time-consuming steps are:\n1. **Loading NWB files** (`pynwb.NWBHDF5IO` and reading large arrays) — I/O bound\n2. **The survey step** — loads every NWB file to gather statistics and reward zone positions\n3. **Full conversion** — loads every NWB file again and extracts all trial data\n4. **Saving the .pkl file**\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The NWB files are large (contain full neural recordings). Conversion is otherwise quite fast\n\n## 13-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. The per-trial loop in `convert_session_data` (lines 267-332) iterates over each trial sequentially. Some operations like `np.digitize` and `compute_distance_to_reward_zone` could theoretically be applied to the full session arrays before splitting into trials, but the variable trial lengths make this awkward. The Viterbi inner loop (lines 503-507) iterates over states, which could be vectorized with matrix operations.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The per-trial loop is the natural structure given variable-length trials. Vectorizing would require padding or masking.\n\n## 13-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\ni. The survey step and the conversion step both load every NWB file and read the same data arrays (neural, behavior). all_info\n\ndef segment_reward_positions(reward_zone_positions):\n    # assign each trial to one of the reward zones defined in reward_zone_dict\n    # use viterbi algorithm with a high cost for switching to encourage stable assignments\n    zone_names = sorted(reward_zone_dict.keys())\n    n_states = len(zone_names)\n    zone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\n    pstay = .9\n    sigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\n\n    # transition log-probabilities\n    log_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\n    np.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\n\n    results = {}\n\n    for mouse_id, positions in reward_zone_positions.items():\n        n_trials = positions.shape[0]\n        startpoints = positions[:,0] # use the start point as it looks cleaner\n        valid = ~np.isnan(startpoints)\n\n        # emission log-probabilities: Gaussian penalty based on distance to zone range\n        # distance is 0 if inside [lo, hi], otherwise distance to nearest edge\n        # for NaN trials, uniform emission (all zeros) so assignment is driven by transitions\n        log_emission = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states))\n        dist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\n                          startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\n        dist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\n        log_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\n\n        # viterbi forward pass\n        log_delta = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states))\n        psi = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states), dtype=int)\n        log_delta[0] = log_emission[0]  # uniform prior\n        for t in range(1, n_trials):\n            for k in range(n_states):\n                scores = log_delta[t - 1] + log_trans[:, k]\n                psi[t, k] = np.argmax(scores)\n                log_delta[t, k] = scores[psi[t, k]] + VR provided tight control over sensory stimuli and the animal’s trajectory, allowing us to observe neuronal remapping in relation to distant rewards, a phenomenon potentially less visible in freely moving scenarios. Furthermore, the task included multiple updates to a hidden reward zone across two environments, allowing us to dissociate spatially driven and reward-driven remapping. Imaging began on day 1 of task acquisition, in which animals traversed a unidirectional 450 cm virtual linear track (for example, Environment 1 (ENV 1)) with a hidden 50 cm reward zone where sucrose water was delivered operantly for licking (Fig. 1d,e). On day 3, the reward zone was moved within a ‘switch’ session to a new track location, signaled by automatic reward delivery on the first ten post-switch trials only if the mouse failed to lick in the new zone. On day 5, the reward zone was moved to a third location, then returned to its original location on day 7. On day 8, the reward switch coincided with the introduction of a novel environment (for example, ENV 2), in which the switch order was then reversed (Fig. 1e). On ‘stay’ days, the last reward location from the previous day was maintained. A separate ‘fixed-condition’ group of mice (n = 3) experienced only one reward location in a single environment (ENV 1) (Extended Data Fig. 1), to control for the effect of experience. To maintain engagement, the reward was randomly omitted on ~15% of trials. At the end of the track, mice passed through a variable length gray ‘teleport’ zone (~50 cm + temporal jitter up to 10 s; Methods) before starting the next lap.\n13:The main ‘switch’ task involved two virtual environments similar to those previously used to study hippocampal remapping, each with visually distinct features from the pre-training environment. Both environments consisted of a 450 cm linear track, with two colored towers (green in ENV 1, blue in ENV 2) and two patterned towers along the walls. Environments were further distinguished by the frequency of diagonal wall gratings (low, ENV 1; high, ENV 2) and color of the sky (dark gray, ENV 1; light gray, ENV 2). The reward zone was a ‘hidden’, unmarked 50 cm span at one of three possible locations along the track, each equidistantly spaced between the towers to control for proximity of each reward to visual landmarks: zone A, 80–130 cm; zone B, 200–250 cm; zone C, 320–370 cm. Only one reward zone was ever active at a time. Reward was randomly omitted on approximately 15% of trials, determined by a random number generator for each trial. Each lap terminated in a black curtain following by a ‘teleport period’ that began with an unchanging gray display for a randomly jittered amount of time (‘jitter period’) between 1 and 5 s (5–10 s on trials following reward omissions or trials in which the mouse did not lick in the reward zone), after which the gray display began to move again for 50 cm giving the appearance of a gray ‘tunnel,’ before the mouse re-entered the virtual environment at 0 cm.\n33:To avoid assumptions about data distributions, we used nonparametric tests or permutation tests in most cases, except when a Shapiro–Wilk test for normality confirmed that parametric tests were reasonable. These models apply warping functions of increasing nonlinear complexity to stretch and compress the data on each trial for maximal alignment. We included both rewarded and omission trials in the fitting procedure to find the best alignment across them. Model fit was assessed using the mean squared error between the time-warped speed profile of each trial and the mean across time-warped trials (Extended Data Fig. 8a). The\nagent's criterion reproduces **exactly 81 trials**, which it treats (Notes Step 4) as simultaneous\nconfirmation of the criterion *and* of the lap segmentation. It notes the one deviation: the reference\nsets those laps' licks to NaN rather than dropping the lap, but \"since `lick` is one of our decoder\noutputs and NaNs are not permitted, dropping the trial is the faithful equivalent\" (Key Decision 5).\nStep 10 Check 5 separately confirms that no lap needs a duration filter (min 96 frames = 6.2 s, max\n3,359 frames = 216.6 s) and that the smallest session still has 40 laps, so every session supports a\ntrain/validation split.\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. The raw suite2p traces: `processing/ophys/Fluorescence/plane*/data` (F) and\n`processing/ophys/Neuropil/plane*/data` (Fneu), restricted to the ROIs with\n`ImageSegmentation/PlaneSegmentation/iscell[:,0] > 0`. Notes Step 4 discrepancy table: \"NWB `Deconvolved` is suite2p's own deconvolution of **raw F**,\nnot of the paper's dF/F\" whereas the Methods say \"the activity rate was extracted by deconvolving\ndF/F ... using OASIS\". How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. `compute_dff()` is a port of `reward_relative.preprocessing.dff` (maximin, single channel).\nPer baseline segment: subtract `0.7 × Fneu`; add the segment's mean neuropil back so the ratio is a\ntrue dF/F; Gaussian-smooth along time with σ = 15 frames; take a 300-frame running minimum then a\n300-frame running maximum (the Methods' 20 s window) as the baseline; form `(F − base)/|base|`;\nsmooth with a σ = 2-frame Gaussian. Segments are individual laps, except on the animal/day\ncombinations transcribed from `teleport_metadata.teleport_sessions`, where the laser was not blanked\nand the segment spans the inter-trial interval plus the next lap. OASIS deconvolution\n(`dcnv.oasis(d, 2000, tau=0.7, 15.5078125)`) is implemented and available via `--signal events`.\n\n**The exported signal is dF/F, not the deconvolved events** (`--signal dff` is the default and is what\nthe full run used: `Converting 152 sessions (signal=dff, workers=12)`).\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_dff(F, Fneu, segments, deconvolve=True):\n    from suite2p.extraction import dcnv\n    f_    = np.full(F.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    fneu_ = np.full(F.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    for lo, hi in segments:\n        f_[:, lo:hi]    = F[:, lo:hi]\n        fneu_[:, lo:hi] = Fneu[:, lo:hi]\n    f_ -= NEU_COEF * fneu_                                  # neuropil_method == 'subtract'\n    dff  = np.full(F.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    spks = np.full(F.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32) if deconvolve else None\n    for lo, hi in segments:\n        x = f_[:, lo:hi] + NEU_COEF * np.nanmean(fneu_[:, lo:hi], axis=1, keepdims=True)\n        flow = gaussian_filter1d(x, BASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=1)   # sigma = 15\n        flow = minimum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)  # 300 frames\n        flow = maximum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n        d = (x - flow) / np.abs(flow)\n        d = gaussian_filter1d(d, DFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=1)           # sigma = 2\n        dff[:, lo:hi] = d\n        if deconvolve:\n            spks[:, lo:hi] = dcnv.oasis(np.ascontiguousarray(d), 2000, TAU, FRAME_RATE)\n    return dff, spks\n```\n```python\nkeep_teleports = S[\"exp_day\"] in TELEPORT_SESSIONS.get(S[\"subject\"], [])\nif keep_teleports:\n    segments = [(si[0], ti[0])]\n    segments += [(ti[k - 1] + 1, ti[k]) for k in range(1, ntrials_raw)]\nelse:\n    segments = list(zip(si.tolist(), ti.tolist()))\n...\nactivity = spks if signal == \"events\" else dff\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 3 quotes the Methods verbatim for every constant, and Step 10 Check 3 tabulates the\nstage-by-stage equivalence with `preprocessing.dff` (\"identical, same constants, same slice-wise\napplication\"). Step 10 Check 2 re-implements dF/F independently (stride-trick min/max, explicit\nGaussian convolution, float64) and matches to 9e-8–3.5e-7.\n\nFor the dF/F-vs-events choice, Notes Step 7 gives a measured comparison on 2- and 6-session subsets:\n\"Deconvolved events are temporally sparse (~77% of frames exactly 0), so a single 64 ms frame carries\nvery little information for [a memoryless per-timepoint linear] model, while dF/F integrates activity\nover the indicator decay.\" dF/F won on every time-varying output (e.g. track_position 0.761 vs 0.697;\ndistance_to_reward_zone 0.560 vs 0.504 on the 6-session set). The agent frames it as \"the deviation\nfrom the paper's *decoding* signal is one the task explicitly allows ('except where ... training a\nneural decoder require otherwise')\" and keeps `--signal events` as a one-flag alternative.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two filters, both the paper's. (1) suite2p manual curation: only `iscell[:,0] > 0` ROIs are read.\n(2) Putative interneurons are removed: the Pearson correlation between each cell's dF/F and the\nanimal's running speed is computed over all **in-trial** samples of the session, and cells with\nr > 0.5 are dropped. The correlation is computed as a single vectorised matrix-vector product rather\nthan a per-cell loop; cells with an undefined correlation (zero variance) are mapped to r = 0 and\nkept. Result: 138,678 `iscell` ROIs → 417 removed (0.30%) → 138,261 exported neurons.\n\nii.\n```python\nin_trial = np.zeros(len(pos), dtype=bool)\nfor lo, hi in zip(si, ti):\n    in_trial[lo:hi] = True\n\nd  = dff[:, in_trial]\nv  = speed[in_trial].astype(np.float64)\ndc = d - d.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)\nvc = v - v.mean()\ndenom = np.sqrt((dc.astype(np.float64) ** 2).sum(axis=1)) * np.sqrt((vc ** 2).sum())\nwith np.errstate(invalid=\"ignore\", divide=\"ignore\"):\n    r_speed = (dc.astype(np.float64) @ vc) / denom\nr_speed = np.nan_to_num(r_speed, nan=0.0)\nkeep_cells = r_speed <= INTERNEURON_SPEED_R      # INTERNEURON_SPEED_R = 0.5\nn_interneurons = int((~keep_cells).sum())\n...\nactivity = activity[keep_cells]\n```\n\niii. Methods (Notes Step 3): manual curation \"eliminated ROIs containing multiple somata or dendrites,\nlacking visually obvious transients ... typical of putative interneurons\", and \"Additional putative\ninterneurons were detected for exclusion ... by a Pearson correlation of >0.5 between their dF/F\ntimeseries and the animal's running speed, excluding 0.42 ± 0.85% of cells\". The agent's measured\n0.35% ± 0.60% across sessions (0.30% overall) is reported as consistent. Notes Step 10 Check 4 also\nflags the one residual mismatch honestly: max neurons/session is 2,341 curated (2,321 after\ninterneuron removal) vs the paper's stated 2,172, with the conclusion that \"discarding real, curated\ncells to reach a number in the text would not be justified\".\n\n## 2-d. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\n\ni. Signed distance in cm from the animal's position to the nearest edge of the active zone:\nnegative before the zone, exactly 0 anywhere inside it, positive past it. Computed per lap from the\nraw position samples, then discretised.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef signed_distance_to_zone(pos, zone_start, zone_end):\n    \"\"\"Signed distance (cm) to the nearest point of the reward zone; 0 while inside it.\"\"\"\n    d = np.zeros_like(pos)\n    before = pos < zone_start\n    after  = pos > zone_end\n    d[before] = pos[before] - zone_start\n    d[after]  = pos[after]  - zone_end\n    return d\n...\nout[0] = bin_distance_to_reward(signed_distance_to_zone(p, zone_start[k], zone_end[k]))\n```\n\niii. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Seven classes via explicit boolean masks: 0: d < −50; 1: −50 ≤ d < −10; 2: −10 ≤ d < 0;\n3: d == 0 (i.e. inside the zone); 4: 0 < d ≤ 10; 5: 10 < d ≤ 50; 6: d > 50. The masks cover the real\nline, so no sample is left unassigned by the `np.empty` allocation.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_distance_to_reward(dist):\n    \"\"\"7 classes; see the Decoder Task specification.\n    0: < -50 | 1: [-50,-10) | 2: [-10,0) | 3: 0 (inside zone) | 4: (0,10] | 5: (10,50] | 6: > 50\n    \"\"\"\n    out = np.empty(dist.shape, dtype=np.int64)\n    out[dist < -50] = 0\n    out[(dist >= -50) & (dist < -10)] = 1\n    out[(dist >= -10) & (dist < 0)] = 2\n    out[dist == 0] = 3\n    out[(dist > 0) & (dist <= 10)] = 4\n    out[(dist > 10) & (dist <= 50)] = 5\n    out[dist > 50] = 6\n    return out\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 restates the Decoder Task bin edges and the agent's mapping of \"0 cm\" to \"d == 0\n(inside zone)\". How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. `compute_dff()` is a port of `reward_relative.preprocessing.dff` (maximin, single channel).\nPer baseline segment: subtract `0.7 × Fneu`; add the segment's mean neuropil back so the ratio is a\ntrue dF/F; Gaussian-smooth along time with σ = 15 frames; take a 300-frame running minimum then a\n300-frame running maximum (the Methods' 20 s window) as the baseline; form `(F − base)/|base|`;\nsmooth with a σ = 2-frame Gaussian. Segments are individual laps, except on the animal/day\ncombinations transcribed from `teleport_metadata.teleport_sessions`, where the laser was not blanked\nand the segment spans the inter-trial interval plus the next lap. OASIS deconvolution\n(`dcnv.oasis(d, 2000, tau=0.7, 15.5078125)`) is implemented and available via `--signal events`.\n\n**The exported signal is dF/F, not the deconvolved events** (`--signal dff` is the default and is what\nthe full run used: `Converting 152 sessions (signal=dff, workers=12)`).\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_dff(F, Fneu, segments, deconvolve=True):\n    from suite2p.extraction import dcnv\n    f_    = np.full(F.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    fneu_ = np.full(F.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    for lo, hi in segments:\n        f_[:, lo:hi]    = F[:, lo:hi]\n        fneu_[:, lo:hi] = Fneu[:, lo:hi]\n    f_ -= NEU_COEF * fneu_                                  # neuropil_method == 'subtract'\n    dff  = np.full(F.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32)\n    spks = np.full(F.shape, np.nan, dtype=np.float32) if deconvolve else None\n    for lo, hi in segments:\n        x = f_[:, lo:hi] + NEU_COEF * np.nanmean(fneu_[:, lo:hi], axis=1, keepdims=True)\n        flow = gaussian_filter1d(x, BASELINE_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=1)   # sigma = 15\n        flow = minimum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)  # 300 frames\n        flow = maximum_filter1d(flow, BASELINE_FILTER_WIN, axis=-1)\n        d = (x - flow) / np.abs(flow)\n        d = gaussian_filter1d(d, DFF_SMOOTH_SIGMA, axis=1)           # sigma = 2\n        dff[:, lo:hi] = d\n        if deconvolve:\n            spks[:, lo:hi] = dcnv.oasis(np.ascontiguousarray(d), 2000, TAU, FRAME_RATE)\n    return dff, spks\n```\n```python\nkeep_teleports = S[\"exp_day\"] in TELEPORT_SESSIONS.get(S[\"subject\"], [])\nif keep_teleports:\n    segments = [(si[0], ti[0])]\n    segments += [(ti[k - 1] + 1, ti[k]) for k in range(1, ntrials_raw)]\nelse:\n    segments = list(zip(si.tolist(), ti.tolist()))\n...\nactivity = spks if signal == \"events\" else dff\n```\n\niii. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two filters, both the paper's. (1) suite2p manual curation: only `iscell[:,0] > 0` ROIs are read.\n(2) Putative interneurons are removed: the Pearson correlation between each cell's dF/F and the\nanimal's running speed is computed over all **in-trial** samples of the session, and cells with\nr > 0.5 are dropped. The correlation is computed as a single vectorised matrix-vector product rather\nthan a per-cell loop; cells with an undefined correlation (zero variance) are mapped to r = 0 and\nkept. Result: 138,678 `iscell` ROIs → 417 removed (0.30%) → 138,261 exported neurons.\n\nii.\n```python\nin_trial = np.zeros(len(pos), dtype=bool)\nfor lo, hi in zip(si, ti):\n    in_trial[lo:hi] = True\n\nd  = dff[:, in_trial]\nv  = speed[in_trial].astype(np.float64)\ndc = d - d.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)\nvc = v - v.mean()\ndenom = np.sqrt((dc.astype(np.float64) ** 2).sum(axis=1)) * np.sqrt((vc ** 2).sum())\nwith np.errstate(invalid=\"ignore\", divide=\"ignore\"):\n    r_speed = (dc.astype(np.float64) @ vc) / denom\nr_speed = np.nan_to_num(r_speed, nan=0.0)\nkeep_cells = r_speed <= INTERNEURON_SPEED_R      # INTERNEURON_SPEED_R = 0.5\nn_interneurons = int((~keep_cells).sum())\n...\nactivity = activity[keep_cells]\n```\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Environment type*?\n\ni. The per-trial median of the environment column, rounded to the nearest integer, then broadcast\nacross all of the lap's timepoints as a constant row of `input`. The environment is constant within a\nlap, so the median is just a robust way of reading that constant.\n\nii.\n```python\nenvironment = np.array([int(np.round(np.median(beh[\"environment\"][lo:hi])))\n                        for lo, hi in zip(si, ti)], dtype=np.int64)\n...\ninp[1] = environment[k]\n```\n\niii. Key Decision 9 (Notes Step 5): \"Per-trial variables are broadcast across the trial's timepoints\nso that `input` is (4, T) and `output` is (6, T)\". The measured range over the full dataset is\n[0.0, 1.0], reported in the conversion summary and the verification log. Step 10 Check 2 verifies\n\"`input[1]` == NWB `environment` on that lap — PASS\".\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Trial number* derived from?\n\ni. The 0-based index of the lap within the session, i.e. the position of the lap in the\n`trial_start`/`teleport` flag sequence. The stored NWB `trial number` column is read but not used as\nthe source; the agent instead verified that the two agree.\n\nii.\n```python\nsi, ti = S[\"trial_start\"], S[\"teleport\"]\nntrials_raw = len(si)\n...\ntrial_number = np.arange(ntrials_raw, dtype=np.int64)\n...\ninp[2] = trial_number[k]\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5: \"trial index in session → `input[2]` `trial_number`: 0-based lap index (verified\nequal to NWB `trial number` at trial start)\". Notes Step 10 Check 5: \"VR `trial number` vs lap index\n— equal in **152/152** sessions → `trial_number` input is unambiguous\". (This is a point where the\nhuman reference found disagreement between the stored `trial number` and `trial_start` and therefore\nalso fell back on the loop index.)\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Trial number*?\n\ni. None beyond the index assignment, broadcast across the lap's timepoints as a float32 constant.\nCrucially the numbering is computed over the **raw** lap list *before* the lick-error laps are\ndropped, so kept laps retain their true within-session lap number (the sequence has gaps where a lap\nwas dropped rather than being renumbered). Range over the dataset: 0–99.\n\nii.\n```python\ntrial_number = np.arange(ntrials_raw, dtype=np.int64)\n...\nfor k, (lo, hi) in enumerate(zip(si, ti)):\n    if lick_error[k]:\n        continue\n    ...\n    inp[2] = trial_number[k]\n```\n\niii. Key Decision 10 (Notes Step 5): \"`trial_number` and `previous_trial_outcome` are computed before\nany trial is dropped, so lap numbering and outcome history stay faithful to what the animal\nexperienced.\" This also keeps `trial_number` consistent with the lap-30 reward-zone switch rule, which\nis indexed on raw lap number.\n\n## 6-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Previous trial outcome* derived from?\n\ni. From the previous lap's reward outcome, which is itself derived from the `Reward` time series'\n**timestamps** (mapped onto the frame grid with `np.searchsorted`) combined with the `reward_zone`\nflag column — i.e. the same `is_reward` vector used for `output[5]`.\n\nii.\n```python\nreward_times = f[\"processing/behavior/BehavioralTimeSeries/Reward\"][\"timestamps\"][:]\n...\nreward_idx = np.searchsorted(timestamps, reward_times)\n```\n```python\n# behavior.get_trial_types: rewarded iff a reward was delivered AND the reward zone\n# was entered on that lap (an omission lap never sets the rzone flag).\nis_reward = np.array([\n    bool(np.any((S[\"reward_idx\"] >= lo) & (S[\"reward_idx\"] < hi)) and np.any(rzone[lo:hi] > 0))\n    for lo, hi in zip(si, ti)], dtype=np.int64)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 maps \"reward delivery of previous lap → `input[3]` `previous_trial_outcome`:\n`isreward[k-1]`\", citing `behavior.get_trial_types`. Notes Step 10 Check 5 verifies the timestamp\nmapping is exact: \"Reward timestamps off the frame grid — none: exact in 152/152 sessions →\n`searchsorted` mapping is exact\".\n\n## 6-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Previous trial outcome*?\n\ni. `prev_outcome[k] = is_reward[k-1]`, broadcast across the lap's timepoints. For the **first lap of a\nsession there is no predecessor, and the agent sets the value to 1 (rewarded)** rather than 0. The\nshift is applied over the raw lap list, so a dropped lick-error lap still supplies the history for the\nlap that follows it.\n\nii.\n```python\n# First lap of a session: the immediately preceding (unrecorded) warm-up laps were\n# rewarded unless randomly omitted, so 1 is the expected value.\nprev_outcome = np.empty(ntrials_raw, dtype=np.int64)\nprev_outcome[0] = 1\nprev_outcome[1:] = is_reward[:-1]\n...\ninp[3] = prev_outcome[k]\n```\n\niii. Key Decision 8 (Notes Step 5): \"First lap's `previous_trial_outcome` = 1 (rewarded). Each imaging\nsession was preceded immediately by 30 warm-up laps on the previous day's reward zone, on which reward\nwas delivered unless randomly omitted (~15%), so 'rewarded' is the expected value. Affects 152 of\n12,135 trials.\" Step 12 Check 1 separately shows the input carries no leakage about the *current* lap:\ncorr(previous_trial_outcome, reward_outcome) = +0.021.\n\n## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Distance to reward zone* derived from?\n\ni. The `behavior/position` column plus the active reward zone for that lap. The reward zone is **not**\ninferred from the data: it is read off the VR **scene name** stored in the NWB `identifier` string,\nusing a port of `reward_relative.behavior.get_reward_zones` — the zone is fixed by the scene, and on a\n\"switch\" scene it changes after lap 30. Zone coordinates are the paper's: A = 80–130, B = 200–250,\nC = 320–370 cm. The empirical `reward_zone` flag column is used only as a *validation* signal, not as\nthe source.\n\nii.\n```python\nREWARD_ZONES = {\"A\": (80.0, 130.0), \"B\": (200.0, 250.0), \"C\": (320.0, 370.0)}\nSWITCH_TRIAL = 30                # behavior.get_reward_zones(change_trial=30)\n\ndef parse_scene(identifier):\n    return identifier.strip(\"/\").split(\"/\")[-1]\n\ndef reward_zone_labels(scene, ntrials, change_trial=SWITCH_TRIAL):\n    parts = scene.split(\"_\")\n    labels = np.empty(ntrials, dtype=\"<U1\")\n    if len(parts) == 2 and parts[1].startswith(\"Location\"):          # Env1_LocationA\n        labels[:] = parts[1][-1]\n    elif len(parts) == 4 and parts[1].startswith(\"Location\") and parts[2] == \"to\":\n        labels[:change_trial] = parts[1][-1]                          # Env1_LocationA_to_B\n        labels[change_trial:] = parts[3]\n    elif len(parts) == 5 and parts[2] == \"to\":                        # Env1_B_to_Env2_C\n        labels[:change_trial] = parts[1]\n        labels[change_trial:] = parts[4]\n    else:\n        raise ValueError(\"Unrecognised scene name: %r\" % scene)\n    ...\n    return labels\n```\n```python\nzone_labels = reward_zone_labels(S[\"scene\"], ntrials_raw)\nzone_start  = np.array([REWARD_ZONES[l][0] for l in zone_labels])\nzone_end    = np.array([REWARD_ZONES[l][1] for l in zone_labels])\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 4: \"Reward zone per trial — code says scene name + switch at trial 30 ... data shows\nposition at the first `reward_zone` flag of each trial is within **8.5 cm** of the predicted zone\nstart for **every trial of every session** ... paper says 'each switch occurred after 30 trials'.\n**Consistent.** Use the reference rule (scene + trial 30); verified empirically.\" The zone-vs-data\ncomparison is also drawn in the `--show-processing` summary figure (\"SANITY: zone from scene name vs.\ndata\"), and Step 10 Check 2 lists \"`output[4]` assigned zone contains the lap's reward-zone entry\nposition — PASS\".\n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\n\ni. Signed distance in cm from the animal's position to the nearest edge of the active zone:\nnegative before the zone, exactly 0 anywhere inside it, positive past it. Computed per lap from the\nraw position samples, then discretised.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef signed_distance_to_zone(pos, zone_start, zone_end):\n    \"\"\"Signed distance (cm) to the nearest point of the reward zone; 0 while inside it.\"\"\"\n    d = np.zeros_like(pos)\n    before = pos < zone_start\n    after  = pos > zone_end\n    d[before] = pos[before] - zone_start\n    d[after]  = pos[after]  - zone_end\n    return d\n...\nout[0] = bin_distance_to_reward(signed_distance_to_zone(p, zone_start[k], zone_end[k]))\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5: \"signed distance to nearest point of the active zone, then 7 bins\", referencing\n`behavior.get_reward_zones` for the zone coordinates. This is the quantity the paper calls\nreward-relative position, in linear rather than circular units as the Decoder Task requires. The\nresulting class distribution, [0.251, 0.102, 0.073, 0.238, 0.021, 0.072, 0.243], is checked in Step 5\nagainst the prior expectation \"~11% of samples in class 3 (inside the 50 cm zone of a 450 cm track,\nmodulated by occupancy)\" — the observed 23.8% reflecting the animals slowing in the zone.\n\n## 7-c. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Seven classes via explicit boolean masks: 0: d < −50; 1: −50 ≤ d < −10; 2: −10 ≤ d < 0;\n3: d == 0 (i.e. inside the zone); 4: 0 < d ≤ 10; 5: 10 < d ≤ 50; 6: d > 50. The masks cover the real\nline, so no sample is left unassigned by the `np.empty` allocation.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_distance_to_reward(dist):\n    \"\"\"7 classes; see the Decoder Task specification.\n    0: < -50 | 1: [-50,-10) | 2: [-10,0) | 3: 0 (inside zone) | 4: (0,10] | 5: (10,50] | 6: > 50\n    \"\"\"\n    out = np.empty(dist.shape, dtype=np.int64)\n    out[dist < -50] = 0\n    out[(dist >= -50) & (dist < -10)] = 1\n    out[(dist >= -10) & (dist < 0)] = 2\n    out[dist == 0] = 3\n    out[(dist > 0) & (dist <= 10)] = 4\n    out[(dist > 10) & (dist <= 50)] = 5\n    out[dist > 50] = 6\n    return out\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 restates the Decoder Task bin edges and the agent's mapping of \"0 cm\" to \"d == 0\n(inside zone)\". The `--show-processing` figure panel 6 plots the continuous signed distance with\ndashed lines at −50/−10/0/10/50 and the discretised class on a twin axis, expressly so the\ndiscretisation can be checked by eye; Step 10 Check 2 re-derives the bins independently (\"`output[0]`\ndistance-to-zone bins — PASS\").\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. No extra alignment. The position slice `p = pos[lo:hi]` uses the identical `[lo, hi)` window as the\nneural slice, on the same frame grid, so output sample *j* and neural sample *j* are the same imaging\nframe.\n\nii.\n```python\nfor k, (lo, hi) in enumerate(zip(si, ti)):\n    ...\n    act = np.ascontiguousarray(activity[:, lo:hi], dtype=np.float32)\n    p = pos[lo:hi]\n    ...\n    out = np.empty((6, T), dtype=np.int64)\n    out[0] = bin_distance_to_reward(signed_distance_to_zone(p, zone_start[k], zone_end[k]))\n```\n\niii. Same rationale as 2-d: the NWB behaviour stream was already resampled onto the imaging frame\nclock by the authors, so identical indexing is identical timing. Verified by the per-session\nprocessing plots and by the independent Step 10 spot checks.\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Absolute position* derived from?\n\ni. The `processing/behavior/BehavioralTimeSeries/position` column (cm along the 450 cm virtual\ntrack), used raw.\n\nii.\n```python\nbeh = {k: b[k][\"data\"][:] for k in\n       [\"position\", \"speed\", \"lick\", \"reward_zone\", \"environment\", ...]}\n...\npos, speed, lick, rzone = beh[\"position\"], beh[\"speed\"], beh[\"lick\"], beh[\"reward_zone\"]\n...\np = pos[lo:hi]\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 maps `behavior/position` → `output[1]` `track_position` with no intermediate\ntransform. Step 10 Check 5 audits the raw values across all 152 files: 366 laps dip to −2.74 cm at\ntrack entry and the maximum is 451.83 cm, both of which the agent verified land in the open end bins.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Absolute position*?\n\ni. None beyond slicing the lap's samples and discretising them. No smoothing, no unwrapping, no\nclipping of the raw values.\n\nii.\n```python\np = pos[lo:hi]\n...\nout[1] = bin_position(p)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5: the track is 450 cm (Methods) and each lap starts at 0 cm, so the raw column is\nalready in the units the Decoder Task asks for. The observed class distribution\n[0.212, 0.177, 0.231, 0.226, 0.154] is compared in Step 5/9 with the expectation of \"roughly\nuniform-ish with more mass in slow (pre-reward) segments\".\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Absolute position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Five equal 90 cm bins via `np.digitize(pos, [90, 180, 270, 360])`, wrapped in a `np.clip(..., 0, 4)`\n(a no-op for four internal edges, but it makes the end bins explicitly open). Samples slightly below\n0 cm fall in class 0 and samples slightly above 450 cm in class 4, rather than forming spurious\nclasses.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_position(pos):\n    \"\"\"5 equal 90 cm bins spanning the 450 cm track.\"\"\"\n    return np.clip(np.digitize(pos, [90.0, 180.0, 270.0, 360.0]), 0, 4).astype(np.int64)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 spells out the intended mapping \"0: p < 90 | 1: 90 ≤ p < 180 | 2: 180 ≤ p < 270 |\n3: 270 ≤ p < 360 | 4: p ≥ 360\", matching the Decoder Task's \"5 equal-sized bins spanning the 450 cm\ntrack\". Step 10 Check 5 confirms the end-bin behaviour on the real out-of-range samples\n(\"Position slightly < 0 at lap start — bin 0, which is correct\"; \"Position slightly > 450 cm — bin 4,\ncorrect\").\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Absolute position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. Identical `[lo, hi)` indexing as the neural matrix; nothing further. Same as 2-d / 7-d. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick* derived from?\n\ni. The `processing/behavior/BehavioralTimeSeries/lick` column, which holds a per-frame **cumulative\nlick count** (not already binary).\n\nii.\n```python\nbeh = {k: b[k][\"data\"][:] for k in\n       [\"position\", \"speed\", \"lick\", \"reward_zone\", \"environment\", ...]}\n...\nout[3] = (lick[lo:hi] > 0).astype(np.int64)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 maps `behavior/lick` → `output[3]` with the transform \"cumulative per-frame lick\ncount → binary (>0)\", citing both the dataset README (\"anything >1 gets set to 1\") and the Methods\n(\"lick counts were converted to a binary vector\"). No temporal smoothing, no\nspatial binning (the paper's lick-rate analyses bin in 10 cm of position, which is not applicable to a\nper-frame decoder output), and no separation of anticipatory vs consummatory licks. Key Decision 5 (Notes Step 5) for the trial removal; Notes Step 5 mapping table for the\nbinarisation. The `--show-processing` panel 8 overlays the raw cumulative count, the exported binary\nand the reward markers so the binarisation and the reward alignment can be inspected together.\n\n## 9-c. How is `output` *Lick* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. Same `[lo, hi)` frame window as the neural data; the lick column is part of the behaviour block\nalready resampled onto the imaging clock and truncated to the common length.\n\nii.\n```python\nout[3] = (lick[lo:hi] > 0).astype(np.int64)\n```\n\niii. As for the other time-varying outputs (2-d). Step 12's reward-zone split analysis on `lick`\n(balanced accuracy 0.700 before the zone vs 0.807 from the zone onward) is used by the agent as\nindirect evidence that lick timing is correctly aligned with neural activity.\n\n## 10-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Reward zone location* derived from?\n\ni. The VR scene name in the NWB `identifier` string, via the same `reward_zone_labels()` port of\n`behavior.get_reward_zones` described in 7-a. The zone label is mapped A → 0, B → 1, C → 2.\n\nii.\n```python\nZONE_TO_IDX = {\"A\": 0, \"B\": 1, \"C\": 2}\n...\nzone_labels = reward_zone_labels(S[\"scene\"], ntrials_raw)\nzone_idx = np.array([ZONE_TO_IDX[l] for l in zone_labels], dtype=np.int64)\n...\nout[4] = zone_idx[k]\n```\n\niii. See 7-a. Additional support in Notes Step 3: \"The reward zone was a 'hidden', unmarked 50 cm span\nat one of three possible locations ... zone A, 80–130 cm; zone B, 200–250 cm; zone C, 320–370 cm\" and\n\"Each switch occurred after 30 trials\". `reward_zone_labels` raises on an unrecognised scene grammar\nor an unknown zone letter, so a mis-parse fails loudly rather than silently mislabelling.\n\n## 10-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Reward zone location*?\n\ni. Parse the scene name into one of three grammars (`Env<n>_Location<Z>`,\n`Env<n>_Location<Z0>_to_<Z1>`, `Env<n>_<Z0>_to_Env<m>_<Z1>`); for the two switch grammars, assign the\nfirst zone to laps 0–29 and the second to laps 30 onwards; map the letter to 0/1/2 and broadcast the\nper-lap value across the lap's timepoints. Lap indices are the raw ones, so the switch lands on the\ntrue lap 30 even if an earlier lap was dropped. Resulting distribution:\n[0.332, 0.336, 0.333] — essentially balanced across A/B/C.\n\nii.\n```python\n    if len(parts) == 2 and parts[1].startswith(\"Location\"):          # Env1_LocationA\n        labels[:] = parts[1][-1]\n    elif len(parts) == 4 and parts[1].startswith(\"Location\") and parts[2] == \"to\":\n        labels[:change_trial] = parts[1][-1]                          # Env1_LocationA_to_B\n        labels[change_trial:] = parts[3]\n    elif len(parts) == 5 and parts[2] == \"to\":                        # Env1_B_to_Env2_C\n        labels[:change_trial] = parts[1]\n        labels[change_trial:] = parts[4]\n    else:\n        raise ValueError(\"Unrecognised scene name: %r\" % scene)\n    unknown = set(labels) - set(REWARD_ZONES)\n    if unknown:\n        raise ValueError(\"Unknown reward zone label(s) %s in scene %r\" % (unknown, scene))\n```\n```python\nout[4] = zone_idx[k]\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 10 Check 4: \"switch at lap **30** in 77/77 switch sessions\", and Step 4's empirical\ncheck that the first `reward_zone` flag of every one of the 12,216 laps falls within 8.5 cm of the\npredicted zone start — i.e. the rule was confirmed against the data rather than assumed.\n\n## 11-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Reward outcome* derived from?\n\ni. The `Reward` time series' **timestamps** (mapped to frame indices with `np.searchsorted` against\nthe behaviour timestamps) **and** the `reward_zone` flag column. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Reward outcome*?\n\ni. Per lap, reduce to a single binary value with `np.any` over the lap's frame window, then broadcast\nthat constant across all of the lap's timepoints (so `output[5]` is a flat row, not an event marker at\nthe reward frame). Computed on the raw lap list so it can also feed `previous_trial_outcome`.\nResulting distribution: 84.2% rewarded / 15.8% omitted, against the paper's \"~15% of trials\" omitted.\n\nii.\n```python\nout[5] = is_reward[k]\n```\n```python\nprint(\"fraction rewarded  : %.4f (mean over sessions)\" % fr.mean())   # 0.8466\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 4: \"Reward rate — `any(reward) AND any(rzone)` per trial — 84.66% rewarded — paper\n'~15%' omitted — **Consistent**.\" Step 12 Check 1 further verifies the schedule is random as the paper\nstates (P(rewarded) = 0.845 / 0.845 / 0.849 for zones A / B / C; near-zero correlation with\ntrial number, environment and previous outcome), and explains the modest decoding accuracy for this\noutput as a task-imposed ceiling (at chance before the animal reaches the zone, 0.654 from the zone\nonward) rather than a conversion error.\n\n## 12. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Several, discovered by an explicit edge-case scan of all 152 files (Notes Step 10 Check 5):\n- **Neural/behaviour length mismatch** (10 sessions have one extra imaging frame): both streams are\n  truncated to the common length.\n- **Trial structure**: assertions that `#trial_start == #teleport`, that each teleport follows its\n  start, that laps do not overlap, and that the last teleport is inside the imaging data. None fired.\n- **Lick-sensor failure** (81 laps): laps dropped (see 1-e).\n- **Undefined speed correlation** (a zero-variance cell would give r = NaN): `np.nan_to_num(..., 0.0)`\n  so such a cell is kept rather than silently dropped.\n- **Non-finite neural samples inside a lap**: hard error rather than silent export.\n- **Out-of-range behaviour values** (position −2.74 to 451.83 cm, negative smoothed speeds down to\n  −6.4 cm/s): absorbed by the open end bins, which the agent verified is the intended class.\n- **Laps with no reward-zone flag at all** (1,822 = 14.9%, the omission laps): `reward_outcome = 0`.\n- **`autoreward` all zeros in every file**: noted and deliberately unused.\n- **No predecessor for the first lap of a session**: `previous_trial_outcome = 1` (Key Decision 8).\n\nii.\n```python\n# A handful of sessions store one extra imaging frame; align to the common length.\nT = min(F.shape[1], len(beh[\"position\"]))\nF, Fneu = F[:, :T], Fneu[:, :T]\nbeh = {k: v[:T] for k, v in beh.items()}\ntimestamps = timestamps[:T]\n\nassert len(trial_start) == len(teleport), \"trial_start/teleport count mismatch\"\nassert np.all(teleport > trial_start), \"teleport must follow its trial start\"\nassert np.all(trial_start[1:] > teleport[:-1]), \"trials must not overlap\"\nassert teleport[-1] <= T, \"trial extends past the imaging data\"\n```\n```python\nr_speed = np.nan_to_num(r_speed, nan=0.0)\n...\nact = np.ascontiguousarray(activity[:, lo:hi], dtype=np.float32)\nif not np.all(np.isfinite(act)):\n    raise RuntimeError(\"non-finite activity in %s trial %d\" % (path, k))\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 10 Check 5 is an explicit table of every edge case the agent looked for, with the\ncount found in the data and the handling chosen.
