How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Two filters, both the paper's. (1) suite2p manual curation: only `iscell[:,0] > 0` ROIs are read.\n(2) Putative interneurons are removed: the Pearson correlation between each cell's dF/F and the\nanimal's running speed is computed over all **in-trial** samples of the session, and cells with\nr > 0.5 are dropped. The correlation is computed as a single vectorised matrix-vector product rather\nthan a per-cell loop; cells with an undefined correlation (zero variance) are mapped to r = 0 and\nkept. Result: 138,678 `iscell` ROIs → 417 removed (0.30%) → 138,261 exported neurons.\n\nii.\n```python\nin_trial = np.zeros(len(pos), dtype=bool)\nfor lo, hi in zip(si, ti):\n    in_trial[lo:hi] = True\n\nd  = dff[:, in_trial]\nv  = speed[in_trial].astype(np.float64)\ndc = d - d.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)\nvc = v - v.mean()\ndenom = np.sqrt((dc.astype(np.float64) ** 2).sum(axis=1)) * np.sqrt((vc ** 2).sum())\nwith np.errstate(invalid=\"ignore\", divide=\"ignore\"):\n    r_speed = (dc.astype(np.float64) @ vc) / denom\nr_speed = np.nan_to_num(r_speed, nan=0.0)\nkeep_cells = r_speed <= INTERNEURON_SPEED_R      # INTERNEURON_SPEED_R = 0.5\nn_interneurons = int((~keep_cells).sum())\n...\nactivity = activity[keep_cells]\n```\n\niii. Methods (Notes Step 3): manual curation \"eliminated ROIs containing multiple somata or dendrites,\nlacking visually obvious transients ... typical of putative interneurons\", and \"Additional putative\ninterneurons were detected for exclusion ... by a Pearson correlation of >0.5 between their dF/F\ntimeseries and the animal's running speed, excluding 0.42 ± 0.85% of cells\". The agent's measured\n0.35% ± 0.60% across sessions (0.30% overall) is reported as consistent. Notes Step 10 Check 4 also\nflags the one residual mismatch honestly: max neurons/session is 2,341 curated (2,321 after\ninterneuron removal) vs the paper's stated 2,172, with the conclusion that \"discarding real, curated\ncells to reach a number in the text would not be justified\".\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Nothing beyond the trial split is needed. The alignment event is the start of the trial, and\nneural and behaviour already live on the same imaging-frame grid in the NWB (the VR stream was\nresampled to the 2P clock by the authors' `vr_align_to_2P`). Every stream for trial *k* is sliced\nwith the same `[lo, hi) = [trial_start[k], teleport[k])` index range, so sample *j* of the neural\nmatrix and sample *j* of every input/output are the same frame. Metadata records\n`off_start = 0.0`, `off_end = None` (laps have variable length).\n\nii.\n```python\nfor k, (lo, hi) in enumerate(zip(si, ti)):\n    ...\n    act = np.ascontiguousarray(activity[:, lo:hi], dtype=np.float32)\n    p   = pos[lo:hi]\n    ...\n    out[2] = bin_speed(speed[lo:hi])\n    out[3] = (lick[lo:hi] > 0).astype(np.int64)\n```\n```python\n\"temporal_alignment_event\": (\n    \"start of trial: the imaging frame at which the mouse enters the linear track at \"\n    \"0 cm (NWB `trial_start` flag). Each trial runs to the `teleport` flag at the end \"\n    \"of the lap, so trials have variable length.\"),\n\"off_start\": 0.0,\n\"off_end\": None,\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 3: \"everything already lives on the imaging frame grid (VR resampled to 2P by\n`vr_align_to_2P`). Trials are laps: `[trial_start, teleport)`.\" The `--show-processing` figures\noverlay raw F, dF/F, events, the exported neural raster, position, distance-to-zone, speed, licks and\nreward markers on one session time axis to make any misalignment visible; Step 12 notes \"reward\nmarkers fall inside the lap they are assigned to, and the exported neural raster has gaps exactly at\nthe ITIs.\"\n\n## 2-e. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. The native per-plane imaging frame: 15.5078125 Hz → **64.4836 ms**, identical for every session\nand animal including the two-plane mice. No rebinning, resampling or smoothing across time bins is\napplied beyond what the dF/F pipeline itself does. The rate is a module-level constant rather than\nbeing read per file; the agent verified separately that the behaviour `dt` is 0.06448363 s in all 152\nsessions and that the two-plane animals store the same number of per-plane frames.\n\nii.\n```python\nFRAME_RATE   = 15.5078125          # Hz, per plane; identical for every session\nFRAME_PERIOD = 1.0 / FRAME_RATE    # s\n...\n\"time_bin_size\": 1000.0 / FRAME_RATE,\n\"sampling_rate_hz\": FRAME_RATE,\n```\n\niii. Key Decision 2 (Notes Step 5): \"Time bin = the native imaging frame, 64.4836 ms, identical for\nall sessions and animals (per-plane rate is 15.5078125 Hz everywhere, including the 2-plane mice).\nThis is the rate the paper's GLM/decoder use ('All behavioral and neural time series were sampled at\n~15.5 Hz'), so no re-binning is applied and no information is discarded.\" Notes Step 4 records the\ncross-check \"behaviour dt = 0.06448363 s in every session; 2-plane animals store the same number of\nper-plane frames → one common time bin for the whole dataset\", and notes that the `rate` stored on\nthe NWB series is the scanner rate (31 Hz on two-plane sessions), which is why the per-plane value is\nthe relevant one for both the time bin and the OASIS kernel.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from start of trial in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. It is **synthesised from the frame index**, not read from the behaviour `timestamps`: frame\nnumber within the lap × the constant frame period (1/15.5078125 s). The agent justified this by first\nestablishing that the behaviour timestamps are an exactly regular grid at that period in all 152\nsessions.\n\nii.\n```python\nFRAME_PERIOD = 1.0 / FRAME_RATE\n...\nT = hi - lo\ninp = np.empty((4, T), dtype=np.float32)\ninp[0] = np.arange(T, dtype=np.float32) * FRAME_PERIOD\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 variable-mapping table: \"frame index → `input[0]` `time_from_trial_start_s`,\n`(i - trial_start_idx) / 15.5078125` seconds\". The premise is the Step 4 finding that the behaviour\nsample interval is 0.06448363 s in every session. Step 10 Check 2 lists \"`input[0]` ==\n`(frame - trial_start)/15.5078125` — PASS\" as an independent re-check.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from start of trial in seconds*?\n\ni. The lap's first frame is time 0 by construction (`np.arange(T)` starts at 0), so the value is\n`0, 0.0645, 0.1290, …`. No offset subtraction, interpolation or smoothing. Stored as float32 in\n`input[0]`, time-varying, one value per frame. Observed range over the whole dataset: [0, 216.536] s.\n\nii.\n```python\ninp[0] = np.arange(T, dtype=np.float32) * FRAME_PERIOD\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5: per-frame time since track entry; the alignment event is trial start so\n`off_start = 0.0`. The maximum of 216.536 s corresponds to the single longest lap (3,359 frames),\nwhich Step 10 Check 5 keeps deliberately: \"the paper applies no duration filter, and the decoder\nhandles variable T\".\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from start of trial in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. By construction: the input array is built with the same length `T = hi - lo` as the neural slice,\nand index *j* of `input[0]` is the *j*-th frame of the same `[lo, hi)` window used for the neural\nmatrix. Before any of this, `load_session` truncates fluorescence and every behaviour column to the\ncommon length `T = min(n_frames, n_behaviour_samples)`, which matters for the 10 sessions that store\none extra imaging frame.\n\nii.\n```python\n# A handful of sessions store one extra imaging frame; align to the common length.\nT = min(F.shape[1], len(beh[\"position\"]))\nF, Fneu = F[:, :T], Fneu[:, :T]\nbeh = {k: v[:T] for k, v in beh.items()}\ntimestamps = timestamps[:T]\n```\n```python\nT = hi - lo\nact = np.ascontiguousarray(activity[:, lo:hi], dtype=np.float32)\ninp = np.empty((4, T), dtype=np.float32)\ninp[0] = np.arange(T, dtype=np.float32) * FRAME_PERIOD\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 3: neural and behaviour share the imaging-frame grid, so no resampling is needed.\nNotes Step 10 Check 5 records the length mismatch as a real edge case found by scanning all 152 files\n(\"Fluorescence one frame longer than behaviour — 10 sessions — truncate to the common length\").\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Environment type* derived from?\n\ni. The `processing/behavior/BehavioralTimeSeries/environment` column (the reference's `morph`\nvariable), 0 = ENV1, 1 = ENV2.\n\nii.\n```python\nbeh = {k: b[k][\"data\"][:] for k in\n       [\"position\", \"speed\", \"lick\", \"reward_zone\", \"environment\", ...]}\n...\nenvironment = np.array([int(np.round(np.median(beh[\"environment\"][lo:hi])))\n                        for lo, hi in zip(si, ti)], dtype=np.int64)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 maps `behavior/environment` → `input[1]` via \"per-trial mode of `morph` (0 = ENV1,\n1 = ENV2)\", citing `behavior.get_trial_types` (which takes `np.unique(morph[firstI:lastI])` per lap).\nNotes Step 4 validates the variable: \"73 sessions all ENV1, 68 all ENV2, 11 sessions contain both\" —\nexactly one cross-environment session per mouse, matching the paper's day-8 environment switch, and\n\"two mice (m17 and m18) began in ENV 2\".\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Environment type*?\n\ni. The per-trial median of the environment column, rounded to the nearest integer, then broadcast\nacross all of the lap's timepoints as a constant row of `input`. Key Decision 9 (Notes Step 5): \"Per-trial variables are broadcast across the trial's timepoints\nso that `input` is (4, T) and `output` is (6, T)\". The measured range over the full dataset is\n[0.0, 1.0], reported in the conversion summary and the verification log. Step 10 Check 2 verifies\n\"`input[1]` == NWB `environment` on that lap — PASS\".\n\n## 5-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Trial number* derived from?\n\ni. The 0-based index of the lap within the session, i.e. the position of the lap in the\n`trial_start`/`teleport` flag sequence. Notes Step 5: \"trial index in session → `input[2]` `trial_number`: 0-based lap index (verified\nequal to NWB `trial number` at trial start)\". Notes Step 10 Check 5: \"VR `trial number` vs lap index\n— equal in **152/152** sessions → `trial_number` input is unambiguous\". (This is a point where the\nhuman reference found disagreement between the stored `trial number` and `trial_start` and therefore\nalso fell back on the loop index.)\n\n## 5-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Trial number*?\n\ni. None beyond the index assignment, broadcast across the lap's timepoints as a float32 constant.\nCrucially the numbering is computed over the **raw** lap list *before* the lick-error laps are\ndropped, so kept laps retain their true within-session lap number (the sequence has gaps where a lap\nwas dropped rather than being renumbered). Range over the dataset: 0–99.\n\nii.\n```python\ntrial_number = np.arange(ntrials_raw, dtype=np.int64)\n...\nfor k, (lo, hi) in enumerate(zip(si, ti)):\n    if lick_error[k]:\n        continue\n    ...\n    inp[2] = trial_number[k]\n```\n\niii. Key Decision 10 (Notes Step 5): \"`trial_number` and `previous_trial_outcome` are computed before\nany trial is dropped, so lap numbering and outcome history stay faithful to what the animal\nexperienced.\" This also keeps `trial_number` consistent with the lap-30 reward-zone switch rule, which\nis indexed on raw lap number.\n\n## 6-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Previous trial outcome* derived from?\n\ni. From the previous lap's reward outcome, which is itself derived from the `Reward` time series'\n**timestamps** (mapped onto the frame grid with `np.searchsorted`) combined with the `reward_zone`\nflag column — i.e. the same `is_reward` vector used for `output[5]`.\n\nii.\n```python\nreward_times = f[\"processing/behavior/BehavioralTimeSeries/Reward\"][\"timestamps\"][:]\n...\nreward_idx = np.searchsorted(timestamps, reward_times)\n```\n```python\n# behavior.get_trial_types: rewarded iff a reward was delivered AND the reward zone\n# was entered on that lap (an omission lap never sets the rzone flag).\nis_reward = np.array([\n    bool(np.any((S[\"reward_idx\"] >= lo) & (S[\"reward_idx\"] < hi)) and np.any(rzone[lo:hi] > 0))\n    for lo, hi in zip(si, ti)], dtype=np.int64)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 maps \"reward delivery of previous lap → `input[3]` `previous_trial_outcome`:\n`isreward[k-1]`\", citing `behavior.get_trial_types`. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Previous trial outcome*?\n\ni. `prev_outcome[k] = is_reward[k-1]`, broadcast across the lap's timepoints. For the **first lap of a\nsession there is no predecessor, and the agent sets the value to 1 (rewarded)** rather than 0. The\nshift is applied over the raw lap list, so a dropped lick-error lap still supplies the history for the\nlap that follows it.\n\nii.\n```python\n# First lap of a session: the immediately preceding (unrecorded) warm-up laps were\n# rewarded unless randomly omitted, so 1 is the expected value.\nprev_outcome = np.empty(ntrials_raw, dtype=np.int64)\nprev_outcome[0] = 1\nprev_outcome[1:] = is_reward[:-1]\n...\ninp[3] = prev_outcome[k]\n```\n\niii. Key Decision 8 (Notes Step 5): \"First lap's `previous_trial_outcome` = 1 (rewarded). Each imaging\nsession was preceded immediately by 30 warm-up laps on the previous day's reward zone, on which reward\nwas delivered unless randomly omitted (~15%), so 'rewarded' is the expected value. Affects 152 of\n12,135 trials.\" Step 12 Check 1 separately shows the input carries no leakage about the *current* lap:\ncorr(previous_trial_outcome, reward_outcome) = +0.021.\n\n## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Distance to reward zone* derived from?\n\ni. The `behavior/position` column plus the active reward zone for that lap. The reward zone is **not**\ninferred from the data: it is read off the VR **scene name** stored in the NWB `identifier` string,\nusing a port of `reward_relative.behavior.get_reward_zones` — the zone is fixed by the scene, and on a\n\"switch\" scene it changes after lap 30. Zone coordinates are the paper's: A = 80–130, B = 200–250,\nC = 320–370 cm. The empirical `reward_zone` flag column is used only as a *validation* signal, not as\nthe source.\n\nii.\n```python\nREWARD_ZONES = {\"A\": (80.0, 130.0), \"B\": (200.0, 250.0), \"C\": (320.0, 370.0)}\nSWITCH_TRIAL = 30                # behavior.get_reward_zones(change_trial=30)\n\ndef parse_scene(identifier):\n    return identifier.strip(\"/\").split(\"/\")[-1]\n\ndef reward_zone_labels(scene, ntrials, change_trial=SWITCH_TRIAL):\n    parts = scene.split(\"_\")\n    labels = np.empty(ntrials, dtype=\"<U1\")\n    if len(parts) == 2 and parts[1].startswith(\"Location\"):          # Env1_LocationA\n        labels[:] = parts[1][-1]\n    elif len(parts) == 4 and parts[1].startswith(\"Location\") and parts[2] == \"to\":\n        labels[:change_trial] = parts[1][-1]                          # Env1_LocationA_to_B\n        labels[change_trial:] = parts[3]\n    elif len(parts) == 5 and parts[2] == \"to\":                        # Env1_B_to_Env2_C\n        labels[:change_trial] = parts[1]\n        labels[change_trial:] = parts[4]\n    else:\n        raise ValueError(\"Unrecognised scene name: %r\" % scene)\n    ...\n    return labels\n```\n```python\nzone_labels = reward_zone_labels(S[\"scene\"], ntrials_raw)\nzone_start  = np.array([REWARD_ZONES[l][0] for l in zone_labels])\nzone_end    = np.array([REWARD_ZONES[l][1] for l in zone_labels])\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 4: \"Reward zone per trial — code says scene name + switch at trial 30 ... data shows\nposition at the first `reward_zone` flag of each trial is within **8.5 cm** of the predicted zone\nstart for **every trial of every session** ... paper says 'each switch occurred after 30 trials'.\n**Consistent.** Use the reference rule (scene + trial 30); verified empirically.\" The zone-vs-data\ncomparison is also drawn in the `--show-processing` summary figure (\"SANITY: zone from scene name vs.\ndata\"), and Step 10 Check 2 lists \"`output[4]` assigned zone contains the lap's reward-zone entry\nposition — PASS\".\n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\n\ni. Signed distance in cm from the animal's position to the nearest edge of the active zone:\nnegative before the zone, exactly 0 anywhere inside it, positive past it. Computed per lap from the\nraw position samples, then discretised.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef signed_distance_to_zone(pos, zone_start, zone_end):\n    \"\"\"Signed distance (cm) to the nearest point of the reward zone; 0 while inside it.\"\"\"\n    d = np.zeros_like(pos)\n    before = pos < zone_start\n    after  = pos > zone_end\n    d[before] = pos[before] - zone_start\n    d[after]  = pos[after]  - zone_end\n    return d\n...\nout[0] = bin_distance_to_reward(signed_distance_to_zone(p, zone_start[k], zone_end[k]))\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5: \"signed distance to nearest point of the active zone, then 7 bins\", referencing\n`behavior.get_reward_zones` for the zone coordinates. This is the quantity the paper calls\nreward-relative position, in linear rather than circular units as the Decoder Task requires. The\nresulting class distribution, [0.251, 0.102, 0.073, 0.238, 0.021, 0.072, 0.243], is checked in Step 5\nagainst the prior expectation \"~11% of samples in class 3 (inside the 50 cm zone of a 450 cm track,\nmodulated by occupancy)\" — the observed 23.8% reflecting the animals slowing in the zone.\n\n## 7-c. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Seven classes via explicit boolean masks: 0: d < −50; 1: −50 ≤ d < −10; 2: −10 ≤ d < 0;\n3: d == 0 (i.e. inside the zone); 4: 0 < d ≤ 10; 5: 10 < d ≤ 50; 6: d > 50. The masks cover the real\nline, so no sample is left unassigned by the `np.empty` allocation.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_distance_to_reward(dist):\n    \"\"\"7 classes; see the Decoder Task specification.\n    0: < -50 | 1: [-50,-10) | 2: [-10,0) | 3: 0 (inside zone) | 4: (0,10] | 5: (10,50] | 6: > 50\n    \"\"\"\n    out = np.empty(dist.shape, dtype=np.int64)\n    out[dist < -50] = 0\n    out[(dist >= -50) & (dist < -10)] = 1\n    out[(dist >= -10) & (dist < 0)] = 2\n    out[dist == 0] = 3\n    out[(dist > 0) & (dist <= 10)] = 4\n    out[(dist > 10) & (dist <= 50)] = 5\n    out[dist > 50] = 6\n    return out\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 restates the Decoder Task bin edges and the agent's mapping of \"0 cm\" to \"d == 0\n(inside zone)\". The `--show-processing` figure panel 6 plots the continuous signed distance with\ndashed lines at −50/−10/0/10/50 and the discretised class on a twin axis, expressly so the\ndiscretisation can be checked by eye; Step 10 Check 2 re-derives the bins independently (\"`output[0]`\ndistance-to-zone bins — PASS\").\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. No extra alignment. The position slice `p = pos[lo:hi]` uses the identical `[lo, hi)` window as the\nneural slice, on the same frame grid, so output sample *j* and neural sample *j* are the same imaging\nframe.\n\nii.\n```python\nfor k, (lo, hi) in enumerate(zip(si, ti)):\n    ...\n    act = np.ascontiguousarray(activity[:, lo:hi], dtype=np.float32)\n    p = pos[lo:hi]\n    ...\n    out = np.empty((6, T), dtype=np.int64)\n    out[0] = bin_distance_to_reward(signed_distance_to_zone(p, zone_start[k], zone_end[k]))\n```\n\niii. Same rationale as 2-d: the NWB behaviour stream was already resampled onto the imaging frame\nclock by the authors, so identical indexing is identical timing. Verified by the per-session\nprocessing plots and by the independent Step 10 spot checks.\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Absolute position* derived from?\n\ni. The `processing/behavior/BehavioralTimeSeries/position` column (cm along the 450 cm virtual\ntrack), used raw.\n\nii.\n```python\nbeh = {k: b[k][\"data\"][:] for k in\n       [\"position\", \"speed\", \"lick\", \"reward_zone\", \"environment\", ...]}\n...\npos, speed, lick, rzone = beh[\"position\"], beh[\"speed\"], beh[\"lick\"], beh[\"reward_zone\"]\n...\np = pos[lo:hi]\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 maps `behavior/position` → `output[1]` `track_position` with no intermediate\ntransform. Step 10 Check 5 audits the raw values across all 152 files: 366 laps dip to −2.74 cm at\ntrack entry and the maximum is 451.83 cm, both of which the agent verified land in the open end bins.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Absolute position*?\n\ni. None beyond slicing the lap's samples and discretising them. No smoothing, no unwrapping, no\nclipping of the raw values.\n\nii.\n```python\np = pos[lo:hi]\n...\nout[1] = bin_position(p)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5: the track is 450 cm (Methods) and each lap starts at 0 cm, so the raw column is\nalready in the units the Decoder Task asks for. The observed class distribution\n[0.212, 0.177, 0.231, 0.226, 0.154] is compared in Step 5/9 with the expectation of \"roughly\nuniform-ish with more mass in slow (pre-reward) segments\".\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Absolute position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Five equal 90 cm bins via `np.digitize(pos, [90, 180, 270, 360])`, wrapped in a `np.clip(..., 0, 4)`\n(a no-op for four internal edges, but it makes the end bins explicitly open). Samples slightly below\n0 cm fall in class 0 and samples slightly above 450 cm in class 4, rather than forming spurious\nclasses.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_position(pos):\n    \"\"\"5 equal 90 cm bins spanning the 450 cm track.\"\"\"\n    return np.clip(np.digitize(pos, [90.0, 180.0, 270.0, 360.0]), 0, 4).astype(np.int64)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 spells out the intended mapping \"0: p < 90 | 1: 90 ≤ p < 180 | 2: 180 ≤ p < 270 |\n3: 270 ≤ p < 360 | 4: p ≥ 360\", matching the Decoder Task's \"5 equal-sized bins spanning the 450 cm\ntrack\". Step 10 Check 5 confirms the end-bin behaviour on the real out-of-range samples\n(\"Position slightly < 0 at lap start — bin 0, which is correct\"; \"Position slightly > 450 cm — bin 4,\ncorrect\").\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Absolute position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. Identical `[lo, hi)` indexing as the neural matrix; nothing further. Because `load_session` first\ntruncates fluorescence and behaviour to a common length, the frame indices refer to the same frames in\nboth streams even in the 10 sessions with an extra imaging frame.\n\nii.\n```python\nT = min(F.shape[1], len(beh[\"position\"]))\nF, Fneu = F[:, :T], Fneu[:, :T]\nbeh = {k: v[:T] for k, v in beh.items()}\n...\np = pos[lo:hi]\nout[1] = bin_position(p)\n```\n\niii. Same as 2-d / 7-d. Additionally, the `--show-processing` figure plots position with the lap\nboundaries and the assigned reward zone overlaid on the same time axis as the exported neural raster,\nwhich is the visual check the agent describes for \"no temporal misalignments\".\n\n## 9-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick* derived from?\n\ni. The `processing/behavior/BehavioralTimeSeries/lick` column, which holds a per-frame **cumulative\nlick count** (not already binary).\n\nii.\n```python\nbeh = {k: b[k][\"data\"][:] for k in\n       [\"position\", \"speed\", \"lick\", \"reward_zone\", \"environment\", ...]}\n...\nout[3] = (lick[lo:hi] > 0).astype(np.int64)\n```\n\niii. Notes Step 5 maps `behavior/lick` → `output[3]` with the transform \"cumulative per-frame lick\ncount → binary (>0)\", citing both the dataset README (\"anything >1 gets set to 1\") and the Methods\n(\"lick counts were converted to a binary vector\"). The same column is what drives the lick-sensor\nerror trial filter in 1-e.\n\n## 9-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick*?\n\ni. Binarisation: any frame with a lick count > 0 becomes 1, otherwise 0. No temporal smoothing, no\nspatial binning (the paper's lick-rate analyses bin in 10 cm of position, which is not applicable to a\nper-frame decoder output), and no separation of anticipatory vs consummatory licks. Laps whose lick\nsensor was stuck are removed entirely (1-e) rather than having their licks NaN-ed, since NaN is not a\nrepresentable output class. list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Distance to reward zone* derived from?\n\ni. Derived from the `position` behavior time series and the reward zone location for the current trial. The reward zone boundaries come from the `reward_zone` behavior time series. This variable is non-zero when the mouse is in the reward zone. I combine this with the position of the mouse when this is non-zero to figure out the closest reward zone. To allow for some noise (of unknown source) and unrewarded tasks, I use the Viterbi algorithm to assign zones so that the rewarded positions match the known reward zones and it is uncommon to switch reward zone. \n\nii. Assigning reward zone location for each trial: \n- Before converting, the `survey()` function was used to try to understand all the data values, including whatever is going on with the `reward_zone` variable. It first computes the position of the min and max position of the mouse when `reward_zone` is non-zero:\n```python\nbehavior_data = nwbfile.processing['behavior']['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series       \ninfo['reward_zone_positions'] = np.full((ntrials, 2), np.nan)\nposition = behavior_data['position'].data[:]\nfor trial in range(ntrials):\n    idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\n    pos_trial = position[idx]\n    reward_zone_trial = reward_zone[idx] > 0\n    if not np.any(reward_zone_trial):\n        continue\n    info['reward_zone_positions'][trial] = [np.min(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial]), np.max(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial])]\n```\nThe function `segment_reward_positions()` uses the Viterbi algorithm to assign reward zone labels so that the initial rewarded positions are close to the corresponding rewarded zone:\n```python\nreward_zone_dict = {'A': [80, 130],\n                    'B': [200, 250],\n                    'C': [320, 370]}\n...\nsigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\nzone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\ndist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\n                    startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\ndist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\nlog_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\n```\nIt also encourages the reward zone label to not change often:\n```python\npstay = .9\nlog_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\nnp.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\n```\n\niii. I plotted the position of the mouse when `reward_zone` was positive (note that the value was between 0 and 6 I think) to determine that the Viterbi approach would likely work, and that the start of the rewarded position was the least noisy variable to use. The class fractions were approximately 1/3 after this, so it seemed correct. \n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\n\ni. For each timepoint, compute the signed distance from the animal's position to the nearest edge of the reward zone. Distance is 0 when inside the zone, negative when before the zone, and positive when past it.  The continuous distance is then discretized into 7 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, inf]`.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef compute_distance_to_reward_zone(position_curr, reward_zone_curr):\n    ntimepoints = len(position_curr)\n    reward_zone_range = reward_zone_dict[reward_zone_curr]\n    distance_to_reward_zone = np.zeros(ntimepoints)\n    idx_before_zone = position_curr < reward_zone_range[0]\n    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_before_zone] = position_curr[idx_before_zone] - reward_zone_range[0]\n    idx_after_zone = position_curr > reward_zone_range[1]\n    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_after_zone] = position_curr[idx_after_zone] - reward_zone_range[1]\n    return distance_to_reward_zone\n\n```\n```python\ndistance_to_reward_zone_bins = [-np.inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, np.inf]\n...\noutput_curr[0] = np.digitize(distance_to_reward_zone, distance_to_reward_zone_bins) - 1\n```\n\n\niii. This matches the paper's concept of distance relative to the reward zone. The reward zone boundaries are from `reward_zone_dict`, inspired by the reference code `Sosa_et_al_2024/src/reward_relative/behavior.py`. The `1e-6` boundary separates exactly 0 (in the zone boundary) from slightly positive. The `-1` corrects `np.digitize` to be 0-indexed.\n\n## 7-c. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. The continuous distance is discretized into 7 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, inf]`.\n\nii.\n```python\ndistance_to_reward_zone_bins = [-np.inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, np.inf]\n...\noutput_curr[0] = np.digitize(distance_to_reward_zone, distance_to_reward_zone_bins) - 1\n```\n\niii. The bin edges match the instructions. The `1e-6` boundary separates exactly 0 (in the zone boundary) from slightly positive. The `-1` corrects `np.digitize` to be 0-indexed.\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The position data and neural data share the same time indices within each trial, so no additional alignment is needed.\n\nii.\n```python\nidx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\nspike_data_curr = spike_data[idx]\nposition_curr = position[idx]\n```\n\niii. Both neural and behavioral data use the same time indexing (verified by timestamp assertions earlier in the code), so indexing by the same `idx` array ensures alignment.\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Absolute position* derived from?\n\ni. Derived from the `position` behavior time series.\n\nii.\n```python\nposition = behavior_data['position'].data[:][:T]\nassert np.allclose(behavior_data['position'].timestamps[:][:T], timestamps), \"Timestamps for position do not match trial number timestamps\"\n...\nposition_curr = position[idx]\n```\n\niii. The `position` variable directly records the animal's position in the VR corridor in cm.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Absolute position*?\n\ni. No processing beyond extracting the per-trial slice and discretizing. Discretized into 5 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, 90, 180, 270, 360, inf]`, corresponding to 90 cm wide bins spanning the 450 cm track. Within the converted trials the position ranges from -0.8 to 451.8 cm, so the open first and last bins absorb the few samples that fall just outside the track (185 of 1,307,665). \n\nii.\n```python\nposition_curr = position[idx]\noutput_curr[1] = np.digitize(position_curr, position_bins) - 1\n```\n\n```python\nposition_bins = [-np.inf,90,180,270,360,np.inf]\n...\noutput_curr[1] = np.digitize(position_curr, position_bins) - 1\n```\n\n\niii. The raw position values are used directly. Each lap starts at 0 cm and the track is 450 cm long (Methods), so five 90 cm bins over 0 to 450 are equal-sized by construction. The survey's wider -50 to 450 range comes from including the inter-trial teleport period, which is not part of any converted trial.\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Absolute position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Discretized into 5 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, 90, 180, 270, 360, inf]`, corresponding to 90 cm wide bins spanning the 450 cm track. \n\nii.\n```python\nposition_bins = [-np.inf,90,180,270,360,np.inf]\n...\noutput_curr[1] = np.digitize(position_curr, position_bins) - 1\n```\n\niii. The instructions specify \"5 equal-sized bins\" spanning the 450 cm track, which is 90 cm per bin. The first and last edges are left open so that samples marginally outside the track fall in the end bins rather than in a class of their own.\n\n## 8-d. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Reward outcome* derived from?\n\ni. Derived from the `Reward` behavior time series. Reward events have their own timestamps.\n\nii.\n```python\nreward_times = behavior_data['Reward'].timestamps[:]\nreward_time_indices = np.searchsorted(timestamps, reward_times)\nisreward = np.zeros(T)\nisreward[reward_time_indices] = 1\n...\noutput_curr[5] = np.any(isreward[idx]).astype(int)\n```\n\niii. Reward event timestamps are mapped to the nearest behavior timepoint using `searchsorted`. For each trial, the output is 1 if any reward event occurred within the trial, 0 otherwise. The value is constant across all timepoints in the trial.\n\nii.\n```python\nreward_time_indices = np.searchsorted(timestamps, reward_times)\nerr = timestamps[reward_time_indices] - reward_times\nassert np.all(np.abs(err) <= time_bin_size/2)\nisreward = np.zeros(T)\nisreward[reward_time_indices] = 1\n...\noutput_curr[5] = np.any(isreward[idx]).astype(int)\n```\n\niii. The alignment error is checked to be within half a time bin. `np.any` is used because a trial either was rewarded or not — the specific timepoint doesn't matter for the per-trial binary output.\n\n## 12. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Several cases are handled:\n- **Neural/behavior length mismatch**: If the number of neural time bins differs from behavior timestamps, data is cropped to the minimum of the two with a warning printed.\n- **Short trials**: Trials with fewer than 50 timepoints (`min_ntimepoints`) are skipped with a warning.\n- **Missing reward zone data**: Trials where `reward_zone` is never active (all zeros) get NaN positions, and the Viterbi algorithm handles these via uniform emission (assignment driven by neighboring trials' transitions).\n- **Reward timestamp alignment**: An assertion verifies reward times align within half a time bin of behavior timestamps.\n\nii.\n```python\nif T != len(timestamps):\n    print(f\"Warning: number of neural time bins ({T}) does not match number of behavior timestamps ({len(timestamps)}), cropping to the minimum of the two\")\n    T = min(T, len(timestamps))\n    spike_data = spike_data[:T]\n    timestamps = timestamps[:T]\n...\nif idx.sum() < min_ntimepoints:\n    print(f\"Skipping trial {trial}...\")\n    istrial[trial] = False\n    continue\n```\n\niii. These are defensive checks found during data exploration. The neural/behavior mismatch occurs in a small number of sessions.\n\n## 13-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. The most time-consuming steps are:\n1. **Loading NWB files** (`pynwb.NWBHDF5IO` and reading large arrays) — I/O bound\n2. **The survey step** — loads every NWB file to gather statistics and reward zone positions\n3. **Full conversion** — loads every NWB file again and extracts all trial data\n4. **Saving the .pkl file**\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The NWB files are large (contain full neural recordings). Conversion is otherwise quite fast\n\n## 13-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. The per-trial loop in `convert_session_data` (lines 267-332) iterates over each trial sequentially. Some operations like `np.digitize` and `compute_distance_to_reward_zone` could theoretically be applied to the full session arrays before splitting into trials, but the variable trial lengths make this awkward. The Viterbi inner loop (lines 503-507) iterates over states, which could be vectorized with matrix operations.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The per-trial loop is the natural structure given variable-length trials. Vectorizing would require padding or masking.\n\n## 13-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\ni. The survey step and the conversion step both load every NWB file and read the same data arrays (neural, behavior). The survey reads neural data to count neurons and check rates, then the conversion reads it again. The `reward_zone_positions` are computed in the survey and then used in the conversion, but other data (position, speed, lick, etc.) is read twice. \n\nii. N/A\n\niii. I don't think these could be run at the same time, as it would require too much RAM. The Viterbi output created during surveying is required to process the data. It was convenient to run the survey before deciding how to handle the conversion of the data. \n\n## 13-d. What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?\n\ni. The upstream `TwoPUtils` package (which builds the\n`sess` class from raw ScanBox + Unity SQLite files) is **not** included, but the NWB files on\nDANDI already contain the product of that stage (VR data resampled onto imaging frames).\n\n### Key Functions Identified\n| Function | File | Stage | Purpose |\n|----------|------|-------|---------|\n| `create_sess` / `append_session_data` | `preprocessing.py` | LOADING | Builds `sess` from raw scan + VR; calls `TwoPUtils.sess.Session.align_VR_to_2P()`. Superseded by the NWB packaging. |\n| `vr_align_to_2P` (TwoPUtils, described in `docs/multi_anim_sess_README.md`) | external | LOADING/ALIGNMENT | Resamples the Unity VR stream onto the imaging frame grid (~15.5 Hz). pos/time linearly interpolated; morph/trialnum/scanning nearest-neighbour; lick/reward/tstart/teleport/rzone integrated-then-differenced so no events are lost; speed = smoothed dz / dt. **This is exactly what the NWB `BehavioralTimeSeries` holds.** |\n| `preprocessing.dff` | `preprocessing.py` | PROCESSING | dF/F per ROI. Neuropil subtraction (`neu_coef=0.7`), per-trial `maximin` baseline (gaussian sigma=15 frames -> `minimum_filter1d(300)` -> `maximum_filter1d(300)`, 300 frames ~= 19.3 s ~ \"20 s window\"), `dff=(F-base)/|base|`, then Gaussian smooth sigma=2 frames, then OASIS deconvolution (`suite2p.extraction.dcnv.oasis`, tau, fs=frame_rate/n_planes). Data **outside trials is set to NaN** so baselines are computed within-trial only. |\n| `utilities.multi_anim_sess` | `utilities.py` | PROCESSING/CURATION | Top-level per-day pipeline: calls `pp.dff(...)` with `neuropil_method='subtract'`, `baseline_method='maximin'`, `deconvolve=True`, then computes place cells and trial metadata. |\n| `utilities.default_dff_method` | `utilities.py` | PROCESSING | `{neuropil_method_red:'subtract', baseline_method:'maximin', neu_coef:0.7, keep_teleports:False}` |\n| `behavior.get_trial_types` | `behavior.py` | PROCESSING | Per-trial `isreward` = `any(reward>0) AND any(rzone>0)` inside `[trial_start_ind, teleport_ind)`; per-trial `morph` = unique VR environment on that trial. |\n| `behavior.get_reward_zones` | `behavior.py` | PROCESSING | Per-trial reward-zone `[start,stop]` coords and labels from the **scene name** in the session metadata; on `X_to_Y` scenes the zone changes at `change_trial=30`. Coordinate dict: label A -> `'X'` = [80,130], B -> `'Y'` = [200,250], C -> `'Z'` = [320,370] cm. |\n| `behavior.correct_lick_sensor_error` | `behavior.py` | CURATION | Sets a trial's licks to NaN when `mean(lick_count > 2) > thr` over the trial (methods text: thr = 0.30). |\n| `behavior.define_trial_subsets` | `behavior.py` | PROCESSING | Splits trials into pre/post-switch sets (not needed for this conversion). |\n| `teleport_metadata.teleport_sessions` | `teleport_metadata.py` | PROCESSING | Animal/day combinations for which the laser stayed on during the teleport ITI -> `keep_teleports=True` in `dff`. This is the reference's `sess.trial_start_inds` /\n`sess.teleport_inds` pair. Alignment event = **start of trial** (entry to the track), so\n`off_start = 0.0` s and `off_end = None` (laps have variable length, 6.2 s - 217 s).\n\n### Variable Mapping\n| Source (NWB) | Target field | Transform | Reference code | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `ophys/Fluorescence/plane*/data`, `ophys/Neuropil/plane*/data`, `ImageSegmentation/.../iscell` | `neural` | keep `iscell==1` ROIs, pool planes; neuropil-subtract (0.7); per-trial maximin dF/F (sigma 15 -> min/max filter 300 frames); smooth sigma 2; OASIS (tau 0.7, fs 15.5078125); drop r(dF/F,speed)>0.5 cells; slice `[start, teleport)` | `preprocessing.dff`, `utilities.multi_anim_sess`, methods \"Calcium data processing\" | shape (n_neurons, T_trial), float32 |\n| frame index | `input[0]` `time_from_trial_start_s` | `(i - trial_start_idx) / 15.5078125` seconds | -- | time-varying |\n| `behavior/environment` | `input[1]` `environment` | per-trial mode of `morph` (0 = ENV1, 1 = ENV2) | `behavior.get_trial_types` | per-trial, broadcast |\n| trial index in session | `input[2]` `trial_number` | 0-based lap index (verified equal to NWB `trial number` at trial start) | -- | per-trial, broadcast |\n| reward delivery of previous lap | `input[3]` `previous_trial_outcome` | `isreward[k-1]`; for the first lap of a session -> 1 | `behavior.get_trial_types` | per-trial, broadcast |\n| `behavior/position` + reward-zone coords | `output[0]` `distance_to_reward_zone` | signed distance to nearest point of the active zone, then 7 bins | `behavior.get_reward_zones` | time-varying |\n| `behavior/position` | `output[1]` `track_position` | 5 equal 90 cm bins over the 450 cm track | -- | time-varying |\n| `behavior/speed` | `output[2]` `speed` | 5 bins: <2, 2-10, 10-20, 20-40, >40 cm/s | 2 cm/s is the paper's own speed criterion | time-varying |\n| `behavior/lick` | `output[3]` `lick` | cumulative per-frame lick count -> binary (>0) | README: \"anything >1 gets set to 1\"; methods: \"lick counts were converted to a binary vector\" | time-varying |\n| scene in `identifier` (+ switch at trial 30) | `output[4]` `reward_zone_location` | A -> 0, B -> 1, C -> 2 | `behavior.get_reward_zones` | per-trial, broadcast |\n| `behavior/Reward/timestamps` + `behavior/reward_zone` | `output[5]` `reward_outcome` | `any(reward in lap) AND any(rzone>0 in lap)` | `behavior.get_trial_types` | per-trial, broadcast |\n| `subject_id` | `subjects` / `subject_idx` | 11 mice | -- | |\n| `ImagingPlane/location` | `brain_regions` = `['CA1']` | all neurons index 0 | paper: dorsal CA1 only; \"planes were pooled for all analyses\" | |\n\n### Discretisation (bin edges exactly as specified in the Decoder Task)\n* `distance_to_reward_zone` d (cm; d<0 before the zone, 0 inside, d>0 past the zone):\n  0: d < -50 | 1: -50 <= d < -10 | 2: -10 <= d < 0 | 3: d == 0 (inside zone) | 4: 0 < d <= 10 |\n  5: 10 < d <= 50 | 6: d > 50.\n* `track_position` p (cm): 0: p < 90 | 1: 90 <= p < 180 | 2: 180 <= p < 270 | 3: 270 <= p < 360 | 4: p >= 360.\n* `speed` v (cm/s): 0: v < 2 | 1: 2 <= v < 10 | 2: 10 <= v < 20 | 3: 20 <= v < 40 | 4: v >= 40.\n* `lick`: 0 / 1.\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Neural signal = OASIS-deconvolved events computed from the authors' dF/F** (not the NWB\n   `Deconvolved`, which suite2p ran on raw F, and not raw F). Rationale: the paper's own decoding\n   (Fig. 3) and GLM are both fit on \"the deconvolved calcium event timeseries\", and the deconvolution\n   removes the asymmetric calcium decay that would otherwise smear a memoryless per-timepoint\n   decoder. dF/F is produced by the same code path and is checked as an alternative in Steps 7-8;\n   the final choice is made on measured decoder accuracy and documented there.\n2. **Time bin = the native imaging frame, 64.4836 ms**, identical for all sessions and animals\n   (per-plane rate is 15.5078125 Hz everywhere, including the 2-plane mice). This is the rate the\n   paper's GLM/decoder use (\"All behavioral and neural time series were sampled at ~15.5 Hz\"), so no\n   re-binning is applied and no information is discarded.\n3. **Trial window `[trial_start, teleport)`**, not the reference's `[start-1, stop-1)`. The reference\n   `dff` shifts every trial window one sample earlier, which includes one pre-track frame (position\n   < 0) and drops the last on-track frame. Because we must align behaviour to neural activity\n   sample-by-sample, we use the behaviourally exact window; the only consequence for dF/F is a\n   one-frame difference in the baseline segment, which is negligible against a 300-frame filter.\n4. **Neuron curation**: `iscell == 1` (the authors' manual suite2p curation, already in the file) and\n   removal of putative interneurons with Pearson r(dF/F, speed) > 0.5, computed over all in-trial\n   samples of the session -- both rules straight from the methods.\n5. **Trial curation**: drop the 81 lick-sensor-failure trials (criterion reproduces the paper's count\n   exactly). The reference NaNs out their licks; since `lick` is one of our decoder outputs and NaNs\n   are not permitted, dropping the trial is the faithful equivalent. No other trials are dropped.\n6. **No <2 cm/s speed mask.** The paper applies it to *spatial* (position-binned) analyses only.\n   Here speed is a decoder output whose lowest class is \"<2 cm/s\", so masking those samples would\n   delete an entire output class. Documented deviation, required by the Decoder Task spec.\n7. **Teleport/ITI periods are excluded** (trials end at `teleport`), matching the reference, which\n   also blanks fluorescence outside laps. `keep_teleports` (reference: ITI included in the *baseline*\n   segment for some animal/day combinations) is implemented so the dF/F baseline matches the paper\n   for those sessions; the extracted samples are in-trial either way.\n8. **First lap's `previous_trial_outcome` = 1 (rewarded).** Each imaging session was preceded\n   immediately by 30 warm-up laps on the previous day's reward zone, on which reward was delivered\n   unless randomly omitted (~15%), so \"rewarded\" is the expected value. Affects 152 of 12,135 trials.\n9. **Per-trial variables are broadcast across the trial's timepoints** so that `input` is (4, T) and\n   `output` is (6, T); the format requires one array per trial and we mix time-varying with\n   per-trial quantities.\n10. **`trial_number` and `previous_trial_outcome` are computed before any trial is dropped**, so lap\n   numbering and outcome history stay faithful to what the animal experienced.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [x] Reward-zone label from scene+trial-30 rule vs. empirical position of the first `reward_zone`\n      flag on every trial (done in Step 4: max error 8.5 cm over all 12,216 trials).\n- [x] Lick-sensor-error trial count == 81 (done in Step 4).\n- [x] Reward rate ~= 85% (done in Step 4: 84.66%).\n- [ ] Totals: 152 sessions, 11 subjects, 12,135 trials after curation, ~138k - interneurons neurons.\n- [ ] Trials/session mean ~= 80.5 +/- 7.4.\n- [ ] Interneuron removal fraction ~ 0.4-1% on average.\n- [ ] Independent re-load sanity checks (Step 10) comparing converted `neural`, `input` and `output`\n      against values read directly out of the NWB with h5py, using `np.allclose`.\n- [ ] Input ranges: time from 0 to trial length; environment in {0,1}; trial_number 0..99;\n      previous outcome in {0,1}.\n- [ ] Output distributions: `distance_to_reward_zone` should have ~11% of samples in class 3\n      (inside the 50 cm zone of a 450 cm track, modulated by occupancy); `track_position` roughly\n      uniform-ish with more mass in slow (pre-reward) segments; `reward_outcome` ~85% class 1;\n      `reward_zone_location` spread over A/B/C.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py`. Run as\n`python -u /app/convert_data.py <outpicklefile> [--full|--sample] [--show-processing]\n[--signal dff|events] [--workers N] [--session-list ids]`.\n\nStructure:\n| Function | Role |\n|---|---|\n| `reward_zone_labels(scene, ntrials)` | port of `behavior.get_reward_zones`: per-trial A/B/C from the scene name, switching after 30 laps |\n| `compute_dff(F, Fneu, segments)` | port of `preprocessing.dff` (maximin, single channel): neuropil subtraction, per-segment baseline, smoothing, OASIS |\n| `load_session(path)` | reads one NWB: pools planes, keeps `iscell==1`, behaviour columns, trial indices, reward times; asserts trial/teleport consistency and truncates to the common length |\n| `convert_session(path)` | baseline segments (honouring `teleport_metadata`), dF/F + events, interneuron removal, per-trial task variables, discretisation, trial assembly |\n| `bin_distance_to_reward` / `bin_position` / `bin_speed` / `signed_distance_to_zone` | output discretisation |\n| `plot_processing(...)` | the `--show-processing` figures |\n| `main()` | parallel driver, summary statistics, pickle writing |\n\nCode efficiencies:\n* Per-session work is fully vectorised over neurons; the only Python loop is over laps\n  (~80 per session), which is unavoidable because baselines are per-lap.\n* `ProcessPoolExecutor` over sessions (default 10 workers); sessions are independent.\n* float32 everywhere (halves memory/IO versus the reference's float64) -- verified in Step 10\n  to make no material difference to dF/F.\n* ROI selection is applied at read time so only `iscell` columns are kept in memory.\n* Timing is printed per session (load / dF/F / total) and for the whole run.\n\nInefficiency identified and fixed: the h5py read `dset[:, :][:, keep]` materialises the whole\n(T, n_roi) block before subsetting. Fancy-indexing h5py directly is *much* slower here (the files\nare contiguous and unchunked), so the full read is deliberate -- 1.8 s for the largest session.\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion Dataset description\n\n### Experiment\nHead-fixed mice run laps (\"trials\") on a 450 cm virtual linear track while CA1 pyramidal neurons\nexpressing GCaMP7f are imaged at ~15.5 Hz. A **hidden 50 cm reward zone** sits at one of three\ntrack locations — **A: 80–130 cm, B: 200–250 cm, C: 320–370 cm** — and sucrose water is delivered\nwhen the mouse licks inside it. Reward is randomly withheld on ~15% of laps. On \"switch\" days the\nzone moves to a new location **after exactly 30 laps**; on day 8 the virtual environment also\nchanges (ENV 1 ↔ ENV 2). Each lap ends with a teleport / inter-trial interval, which is **not**\npart of the exported trials.\n\n### Scale\n| | |\n|---|---|\n| Subjects | 11 mice (m3, m4, m7, m11, m12, m13, m14, m15, m17, m18, m19) |\n| Sessions | 152 (14 per mouse; m11 has 12 — imaging started on day 3) |\n| Trials (laps) | 12,135 (12,216 in the source, 81 removed for lick-sensor failure) |\n| Neurons | 138,261 total; 154–2,321 per session (mean 910) |\n| Timepoints | 2,576,026 (mean 212 / trial ≈ 13.7 s) |\n| Brain region | dorsal CA1 (single region) |\n| Time bin | 64.4836 ms (the native imaging frame, 15.5078125 Hz), identical for every session |\n\n### Neural signal\n**ΔF/F**, computed with the paper's own pipeline:\nsuite2p `F` and `Fneu` → neuropil subtraction (coefficient 0.7) → per-trial *maximin* baseline\n(Gaussian σ = 15 frames, then 300-frame minimum and maximum filters ≈ 19.3 s) →\n`(F − baseline) / |baseline|` → Gaussian smoothing (σ = 2 frames ≈ 0.129 s).\nDeconvolved OASIS \"events\" can be produced instead with `--signal events` (see\n`CONVERSION_NOTES.md` Step 7 for why ΔF/F is the default).\n\n### Curation applied\n* ROIs: suite2p manual curation (`iscell == 1`); imaging planes pooled for the two 2-plane mice.\n* Putative interneurons removed: Pearson r(ΔF/F, running speed) > 0.5 (417 cells, 0.35% ± 0.60%\n  per session).\n* Trials: 81 laps with lick-sensor failure removed (>30% of the lap's frames with a cumulative\n  lick count > 2) — exactly the 81 laps the paper reports.\n\n---\n\n## 2. How to load and use\n\n```python\nimport pickle\nwith open('/app/converted_data.pkl', 'rb') as f:\n    data = pickle.load(f)\n\nsession, trial = 0, 5\nX = data['neural'][session][trial]   # (n_neurons, T)  float32  ΔF/F\nU = data['input'][session][trial]    # (4, T)          float32\nY = data['output'][session][trial]   # (6, T)          int64    class labels\n\nprint(data['subjects'][data['subject_idx'][session]])       # mouse id\nprint(data['metadata']['session_info'][session]['scene'])   # e.g. 'Env1_LocationB_to_A'\n```\n\nTrain / evaluate the reference decoder:\n\n```bash\npython train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --verify-only    # format + summary\npython train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --plot-samples   # full training (~7 min, GPU)\n```\n\nRegenerate the dataset:\n\n```bash\npython -u /app/convert_data.py /app/converted_data.pkl --full --workers 12    # ~45 s\npython -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing\n```\n\n---\n\n## 3. Output format specification\n\nTop-level keys follow the required schema exactly.\n\n| Key | Type | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|\n| `neural` | list[152] of list[n_trials] of `(n_neurons, T)` float32 | ΔF/F per trial |\n| `input` | list[152] of list[n_trials] of `(4, T)` float32 | decoder inputs |\n| `output` | list[152] of list[n_trials] of `(6, T)` int64 | decoder targets (class indices) |\n| `subjects` | list[11] of str | mouse ids |\n| `subject_idx` | `(152,)` int64 | index into `subjects` per session |\n| `brain_regions` | `['CA1']` | |\n| `brain_region_idx` | list[152] of `(n_neurons,)` int64 | all zeros (single region) |\n| `input_names`, `output_names`, `output_values` | | names / class labels |\n| `metadata` | dict | see below |\n\n### Trials and alignment\nEach trial is one lap, from the NWB `trial_start` flag (entry to the track at 0 cm) up to but not\nincluding the `teleport` flag. Alignment event = **trial start**, so\n`metadata['off_start'] = 0.0` and `metadata['off_end'] = None` (laps have variable length:\n96–3,359 frames, 6.2–216.6 s).\n\n### Inputs (`input_names`)\n| idx | Name | Type | Range |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | `time_from_trial_start_s` | time-varying, seconds | 0 – 216.5 |\n| 1 | `environment` | per trial (broadcast) | 0 = ENV 1, 1 = ENV 2 |\n| 2 | `trial_number` | per trial (broadcast) | 0 – 99, 0-based lap index |\n| 3 | `previous_trial_outcome` | per trial (broadcast) | 0 = omitted, 1 = rewarded (first lap of a session = 1) |\n\n### Outputs point of the active zone (0 while inside): `<-50`, `[-50,-10)`, `[-10,0)`, `0`, `(0,10]`, `(10,50]`, `>50` | 0.251, 0.102, 0.073, 0.239, 0.021, 0.072, 0.243 |\n| 1 | `track_position` | 5 | 90 cm bins over the 450 cm track | 0.212, 0.177, 0.231, 0.226, 0.154 |\n| 2 | `speed` | 5 | `<2`, `2–10`, `10–20`, `20–40`, `>40` cm/s | 0.117, 0.087, 0.134, 0.319, 0.343 |\n| 3 | `lick` | 2 | ≥1 lick detected in the frame | 0.777, 0.223 |\n| 4 | `reward_zone_location` | 3 | A / B / C, per trial | 0.332, 0.336, 0.333 |\n| 5 | `reward_outcome` | 2 | reward delivered on this lap, per trial | 0.158, 0.842 |\n\n### `metadata`\n`task_description`, `time_bin_size` (64.4836 ms), `temporal_alignment_event`, `off_start`,\n`off_end`, `neural_signal`, `neural_processing`, `neuron_curation`, `trial_curation`,\n`sampling_rate_hz`, `recording_modality`, `species`, `reference`, and `session_info` — a list of\n152 dicts with, per session: `session_id`, `subject`, `exp_day`, `scene`, `date`, `region`,\n`n_roi_total`, `n_roi_iscell`, `n_interneurons_removed`, `n_neurons`, `n_trials_raw`, `n_trials`,\n`n_trials_lick_error`, `keep_teleports`, `frac_rewarded`, `reward_zones`,
